messages.content: I want to determine when unpaired RNA and chromatin accessibility measurements support transferable perturbation-response prediction, despite donor–batch confounding. The performance requirement is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations. I also want to characterize the identifiability assumptions that separate biological coupling from batch effects, including cases where that separation is impossible.

Those are two related but distinct questions. The predictive question asks whether adding chromatin accessibility measurements improves perturbation-response accuracy beyond RNA-only models under the stated unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation conditions. The identifiability question asks what would justify interpreting a cross-modality relationship as biological coupling rather than a pattern induced by batch. A lower RMSE would address predictive performance; by itself, it would not establish that the inferred coupling is uniquely biological.
What exactly is difficult about the measurements being unpaired?

Unpaired means the RNA and chromatin accessibility measurements do not supply a direct observation of both modalities for each matched unit. Consequently, correspondence between their patterns must be inferred rather than read from observed pairs. More than one correspondence could be consistent with the separate measurements, especially if donor and batch also structure what is observed. That uncertainty matters both for prediction and for claims about what the relationship represents.
So I should not treat a shared-looking pattern across the two modalities as proof of biological coupling?

Right. A pattern that looks shared could be consistent with biological coupling, but it could also reflect batch-associated variation or a combination of the two. The key question is whether the available variation and stated assumptions distinguish those explanations. If they do not, the same observed patterns may admit multiple interpretations.
Can you explain donor–batch confounding without assuming anything particular about these measurements?

At a general level, donor–batch confounding means donor identity and batch assignment vary together in a way that makes their contributions hard to disentangle. If a pattern differs across donors but those donors are also distinguished by batch, attributing the pattern specifically to donor biology rather than batch requires further information or assumptions. The problem is especially relevant here because an apparent relationship between RNA and accessibility could inherit that ambiguity.
What sort of assumptions would have to be made explicit?

The account would need to state what is assumed to remain biological and transferable across donors, perturbations, and batches, and what kinds of variation are permitted to be batch effects. It would also need to explain what information, if any, distinguishes those components in unpaired measurements. Possible identifying conditions, in the abstract, include variation that breaks the donor–batch association or independent constraints on batch effects. Those are examples of conditions to examine, not assertions that they hold here.
And I need to describe circumstances in which those assumptions cannot resolve the ambiguity?

Yes. For example, if donor and batch are perfectly linked and there is no other information that constrains either effect, a donor-associated difference and a batch-associated difference can be observationally indistinguishable. Unpaired measurements can introduce another ambiguity: separate RNA and accessibility patterns need not determine a unique biological correspondence between them. In such cases, one should say that separation is not identifiable under the available information and assumptions, rather than assign a definitive biological interpretation.
Does an impossible-to-separate case mean transferable prediction is impossible too?

Not necessarily. Identifiability of the biological explanation and predictive accuracy are different properties. A relationship could help predict responses without uniquely revealing why it works. Conversely, a plausible biological interpretation does not guarantee the required accuracy on unseen donors and perturbations. The distinction is important: predictive success would need to be assessed by the stated RMSE comparison, while interpretive claims would need their own explicit assumptions.
How should I read the 15% requirement precisely?

It is a relative reduction in perturbation-response RMSE against the RNA-only comparison: an RMSE 15% lower corresponds to 0.85 times the RNA-only RMSE for the same comparison. The condition concerns unseen donors and perturbations, so performance on already-seen donors or perturbations would not, by itself, establish that requirement. Nothing in the goal says the reduction has already been achieved.
Why specify RNA-only models as the comparison?

That comparison isolates the practical question of whether access to chromatin accessibility measurements adds predictive value beyond RNA measurements alone. The requirement is not merely that a model using both modalities predicts responses; it is that its perturbation-response RMSE be reduced by 15% versus RNA-only models under the stated unseen conditions.
Could a better RMSE be described as evidence that the modalities are biologically coupled?

It could be consistent with useful cross-modality information, but it should not automatically be described as identifying biological coupling. Prediction may benefit from a signal whose origin remains ambiguous under donor–batch confounding. A careful account would report the predictive comparison separately from the assumptions needed to interpret the signal as biological rather than batch-related.
What would it mean for the prediction to be transferable, rather than just accurate in a narrower setting?

Here, transferability is tied to the stated unseen donors and perturbations. The aim is not only to fit relationships within familiar observations, but to have them remain useful for predicting perturbation responses when the donor and perturbation are unseen. That is why the evaluation condition is part of the goal, rather than an incidental detail of the RMSE figure.
Is it fair to frame the work as asking when the accessibility measurements help, and when they cannot be interpreted cleanly?

Yes, with one nuance: predictive usefulness and clean interpretation need not coincide. The full question is when unpaired RNA and chromatin accessibility measurements support the specified improvement in transferable perturbation-response prediction, what assumptions would permit biological coupling to be distinguished from batch effects, and where the available information leaves that distinction impossible.
I want the account to be candid if the data support only prediction and not a unique explanation.

That is consistent with the goal. It leaves room to assess whether the 15% RMSE reduction versus RNA-only models occurs on unseen donors and perturbations, while separately stating the limits of identifiability. In an ambiguous case, the appropriate conclusion would be about what the measurements and assumptions do or do not distinguish—not a stronger claim that biological coupling has been isolated.

As a way to pursue this, I propose fitting a batch-aware latent RNA–ATAC alignment through shared cell-state anchors, testing donor and perturbation holdouts, and flagging rank-deficient donor–batch designs. How do those pieces fit together?

The alignment is a proposed way to relate the unpaired RNA and ATAC measurements: shared cell-state anchors provide a basis for connecting their latent representations, while the batch-aware aspect acknowledges that batch variation could otherwise be mistaken for cross-modality structure. Donor and perturbation holdouts address whether the resulting predictions transfer beyond the observations used to fit the relationship. Flagging rank-deficient donor–batch designs addresses a different question: whether the design contains enough independent information to separate donor-associated variation from batch-associated variation.
Does calling them shared cell-state anchors imply the RNA and ATAC measurements are paired?

No. An anchor is a proposed point of correspondence at the level of cell state; it is not, by itself, an observed RNA–ATAC pair. In unpaired measurements, relying on anchors still requires assumptions about which states correspond across modalities. The alignment should not be described as directly observed pairing.
What does “latent” add to the proposal?

It means the proposed alignment relates the modalities through a representation of cell state rather than requiring their raw measurements to match directly. That can express a hypothesized common structure despite the measurements being different. But a latent representation does not automatically identify which parts of that structure are biological and which are associated with batch.
Then what should “batch-aware” mean without implying that the confounding has been solved?

It means the fitting and interpretation explicitly account for batch as a possible source of variation in the RNA–ATAC relationship. It is a feature of the proposed approach, not a guarantee that batch effects can be separated from biology. Where donor and batch lack distinguishable variation, acknowledging batch cannot create the missing information.
Why specifically flag rank-deficient donor–batch designs?

Rank deficiency signals that the donor–batch structure does not supply independent information for all the distinctions one might try to make. If donor and batch are inseparable within that structure, an apparent donor-associated pattern can also be explained as batch-associated. A flag would make that limitation visible rather than allowing an alignment or prediction to be interpreted as if the design had resolved it.
Would the flag mean I have to discard any prediction from such a design?

The proposal says to flag those designs, not to discard them. The flag concerns what can be identified about donor versus batch effects. Predictive performance is a separate matter to assess with the holdouts; even a useful prediction would not, on its own, remove an identifiability warning.
How do the holdouts relate to the RMSE goal?

Donor and perturbation holdouts are intended to test transfer to unseen donors and perturbations, which is the setting of the stated performance requirement. The relevant comparison remains perturbation-response RMSE against RNA-only models, with a 15% reduction as the target. The proposal sets out a way to test that requirement; it does not say the target has been met.
Could a holdout result establish that the anchors captured biological coupling rather than batch?

Not by itself. A holdout tests predictive generalization under the conditions it represents. Interpreting the alignment as biological coupling still depends on whether the anchors and donor–batch structure permit that distinction. Strong prediction and a rank-deficiency warning could therefore coexist without contradiction.
Is a rank-deficient design the only situation in which interpretation might be ambiguous?

No. It is one explicitly proposed warning about donor–batch separation. Unpaired measurements also leave the proposed RNA–ATAC correspondence dependent on the validity and distinctiveness of the shared cell-state anchors. Flagging rank deficiency is useful, but absence of that particular flag would not, by itself, prove that the latent alignment has a unique biological interpretation.
So the proposal has a predictive check and an interpretive check, rather than one check doing both jobs?

Exactly. Fitting the batch-aware latent alignment via shared cell-state anchors provides a candidate cross-modality relationship. Donor and perturbation holdouts test its transferable predictive value. Flagging rank-deficient donor–batch designs highlights a condition under which separating biological coupling from batch effects may be impossible without additional information or assumptions. None of those steps should be reported as a completed result at this stage.
Which donor–batch incidence patterns would make shared-anchor RNA–ATAC coupling identifiable, and when would complete donor nesting make separation impossible?

It helps to distinguish two things: whether the donor–batch pattern permits donor and batch contributions to be separated, and whether shared cell-state anchors identify an RNA–ATAC relationship as biological. A design in which donors appear across batches can provide the overlap needed for the first distinction. But incidence alone cannot establish the second: the anchors must genuinely connect comparable states across the unpaired modalities, and the assumed form of batch effects matters.
What do you mean by incidence here?

It is simply the pattern of which donors have measurements in which batches, without making any claim about the measurements themselves. You can picture donors and batches as two sets of points, with a link wherever a donor appears in a batch. Links crossing between batches create opportunities to compare a donor across batch contexts; complete nesting means each donor appears in only one batch.
Is it enough for at least one donor to occur in more than one batch?

Not necessarily for every distinction of interest. Such a donor supplies a bridge between the batches it connects, but other batches might still have no link to that part of the design. Under an additive donor-plus-batch account, a connected incidence pattern supports relative comparisons across the connected design, subject to a reference convention. Disconnected portions retain separate ambiguities. And even a connected pattern does not establish that an inferred RNA–ATAC alignment reflects biological coupling.
Could you give a purely illustrative incidence pattern that has that bridging property?

For example, imagine one donor observed in two batches, and another donor observed in the second and a third batch. Those overlaps create a chain of comparisons across the three batches. This is only a schematic example of incidence, not a description of the available measurements or a guarantee of identifiability: the conclusion still depends on what effects are allowed and whether the relevant cell-state anchors can be compared.
What goes wrong if every donor is completely nested in a single batch?

With complete nesting, no donor is observed in a second batch, so the incidence pattern offers no within-donor contrast across batches. If donor and batch can each contribute an otherwise unrestricted fixed effect, a batch-associated shift can be reassigned to the donor effects for donors in that batch without changing the observations. The design therefore cannot uniquely separate those contributions on its own. Having multiple donors in a batch does not remove that particular fixed-effect ambiguity.
Is that impossibility absolute, or does it depend on the assumptions?

It depends on what is being claimed and assumed. Complete nesting makes separation impossible from incidence alone when donor and batch effects are both unrestricted in that sense. A stronger assumption that constrains one of those effects could produce an estimate, but the distinction would then rely on the assumption rather than on a donor appearing across batches. It would be misleading to call that assumption-dependent estimate a separation demonstrated by the nested design itself.
Does complete nesting also prove that no part of the RNA–ATAC coupling can be learned?

No. The impossibility just described concerns separating unrestricted donor and batch contributions. Some cross-modality predictive relationship might still be estimated under additional assumptions, including assumptions about shared cell-state anchors and which relationships remain stable. The narrower point is that a relationship observed under complete nesting cannot, merely by virtue of that incidence pattern, be uniquely attributed to biological coupling rather than donor-linked batch structure.
How do the shared anchors affect the incidence argument?

They provide the proposed basis for aligning unpaired RNA and ATAC at the level of cell state. For that basis to help identify biological coupling, the anchors must supply meaningful correspondences that are not equally explained by batch-associated patterns. Donor–batch overlap can help distinguish certain donor and batch contributions, but it cannot repair anchors that fail to distinguish comparable biological states across the modalities. Conversely, plausible anchors do not create a missing donor-across-batch comparison.
So even a well-connected donor–batch pattern is not a standalone proof?

Correct. Connectivity is an incidence property. Under a specified additive-effects interpretation, it can make relative donor and batch contrasts estimable where nesting cannot. But if batch effects are allowed to mimic arbitrary state-dependent changes, or the unpaired anchors admit multiple equally consistent alignments, connectivity alone does not identify a unique biological RNA–ATAC coupling. The scope of an identifiability statement must include those modeling assumptions.
Can the rank-deficiency flag capture the complete-nesting problem?

Yes, for a donor–batch design that attempts to represent separate unrestricted donor and batch effects, complete nesting creates a linear dependency: each batch indicator can be expressed using the indicators for the donors nested within it. Flagging that deficiency makes the lack of independent donor–batch information explicit. The flag diagnoses a limitation of that separation; it does not by itself evaluate the accuracy of perturbation-response predictions.
Would donor and perturbation holdouts answer the incidence question?

They answer a different question: whether prediction transfers to unseen donors and perturbations, including whether it reaches the stated 15% perturbation-response RMSE reduction versus RNA-only models. Holdout performance cannot make a rank-deficient donor–batch design full rank or establish a unique biological interpretation of the anchors. Both the predictive check and the incidence-and-assumption check are needed for their respective claims.
How should I phrase the answer to the question without claiming more than the incidence pattern supports?

You could frame it conditionally: overlapping, connected donor–batch incidence can support separation of relative donor and batch effects under an explicitly restricted model, while shared-anchor RNA–ATAC coupling additionally requires defensible cross-modality correspondences and assumptions that distinguish biological structure from batch variation. With complete donor nesting, unrestricted donor and batch effects are not separately identifiable from the incidence pattern, so attributing an apparent coupling uniquely to biology rather than batch is not justified on that basis alone.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: under additive batch effects, invariant shared cell-state anchors and crossed donor–batch observations identify RNA–ATAC coupling; with donors nested in batches, donor and batch are confounded. Can you unpack exactly what that claims?

It is a conditional identifiability hypothesis, not a finding that the coupling has already been identified. Additive batch effects limit how batch can alter the measurements. Invariant anchors supply a stable basis for relating cell states across unpaired RNA and ATAC measurements. Crossed donor–batch observations supply comparisons that can help distinguish donor-associated from batch-associated variation. The contrasting claim is that, when donors are nested in batches, the incidence pattern itself does not separate donor from batch.
Why is additivity important to the hypothesis?

Additivity restricts batch effects to contributions that can be distinguished from the biological relationship under the other stated conditions. If batch were permitted to reproduce arbitrary changes in the apparent RNA–ATAC relationship, the same observations could admit a batch-based explanation and a biological one. Crossing and anchors would then not necessarily distinguish them. The hypothesis therefore depends on the additive restriction; it should not be read as a claim about unrestricted batch effects.
What work does anchor invariance do beyond having anchors at all?

The anchors are the proposed correspondences through which unpaired RNA and ATAC measurements are aligned. Invariance means those correspondences are assumed to retain their relevant cell-state meaning across the comparisons used for identification. Without that stability, an apparent change in the alignment might reflect a changed anchor rather than a batch effect or biological coupling. Calling an anchor invariant is an assumption in this hypothesis, not something established merely by naming it an anchor.
Does invariance mean RNA and ATAC must have identical measurements at an anchor?

No. RNA and chromatin accessibility are different measurements. The claim is about a stable correspondence in cell state, not equality of the measured values. In an unpaired setting, that correspondence has to be justified or assumed; it is not a directly observed RNA–ATAC pair.
What qualifies as crossed donor–batch observations in this argument?

The relevant feature is overlap that lets donor and batch vary separately—for example, observing a donor across batch contexts rather than having each donor confined to just one batch. Those observations create contrasts that a wholly nested pattern lacks. The claim still depends on whether the crossing connects the parts of the design for which separation is sought; the word “crossed” should not be treated as a guarantee that every possible contrast is supported.
Could you explain the contrast that crossing provides without specifying a particular analysis?

Conceptually, observing the same donor in more than one batch offers a way to compare batches without changing donor identity. Having relevant overlap among donors and batches can then link such comparisons across the incidence pattern. Under an additive account, that helps distinguish a batch-associated contribution from a donor-associated one. It does not, by itself, verify the assumed additivity or the invariance of the anchors.
When the hypothesis says the coupling is identified, is that an absolute statement?

No. It means identified within the hypothesized conditions: additive batch effects, invariant anchors, and sufficiently crossed donor–batch observations. It should also be understood relative to whatever aspects of an alignment can be distinguished under those assumptions, rather than as a claim that every imaginable biological mechanism is uniquely recovered. If an assumption fails or the crossing is insufficient for a desired contrast, the claimed separation need not follow.
Now take the nested case. What is the specific ambiguity?

If each donor occurs in only one batch, there is no observation of that same donor under a different batch assignment. With unrestricted donor and batch contributions, a difference associated with a batch can also be assigned to the donors observed in that batch without changing what is observed. Thus the nested incidence pattern does not independently determine how much of such a difference belongs to donor and how much to batch.
Does the nested part of the hypothesis require assuming additive effects too?

The donor–batch ambiguity is already apparent under an additive description if both donor and batch contributions are free to vary: nesting makes those contributions inseparable from the incidence pattern alone. Constraints imposed from outside that pattern could assign them distinct values, but the assignment would rely on those constraints. The hypothesis contrasts crossing that can support separation under its assumptions with nesting that confounds donor and batch.
Suppose the anchors are invariant even in a nested design. Would that remove the donor–batch ambiguity?

Anchor invariance would address the stability of the proposed RNA–ATAC correspondence; it would not create a missing observation of a donor across batches. A nested design can therefore retain donor–batch confounding even if the anchors behave as assumed. The two conditions serve different roles in the hypothesis and neither can simply substitute for the other.
And could a crossed design compensate for anchors that are not invariant?

Not under this hypothesis. Crossing can provide information about donor and batch contributions, but an unstable anchor may undermine what is being aligned between RNA and ATAC. One could then mistake a change in correspondence for a change in biological coupling or a batch-associated pattern. The proposed identification relies on both kinds of structure being present.
Would successful prediction on donor and perturbation holdouts verify this hypothesis?

It would address transferable predictive performance, not verify the identifying assumptions by itself. A model could predict perturbation responses well while the biological interpretation of its RNA–ATAC relationship remains ambiguous. The hypothesis specifically concerns when coupling can be separated from donor–batch effects; predictive accuracy and that separation are different claims.
How would you state the hypothesis carefully in one sentence?

The hypothesis is that, when batch effects are additive, shared cell-state anchors are invariant, and donor–batch observations are sufficiently crossed, biological RNA–ATAC coupling can be distinguished from donor and batch variation; with donors completely nested in batches, donor and batch contributions remain confounded by the incidence pattern.

I want to plan a simulation that compares crossed and nested donor–batch layouts, varies whether the shared cell-state anchors are invariant, and quantifies coupling identifiability with profile likelihood and held-out RMSE. How should I think about the roles of those pieces?

The layouts probe what the donor–batch incidence pattern contributes: crossing can supply donor-across-batch contrasts, whereas nesting removes them. Varying anchor invariance probes whether the proposed RNA–ATAC correspondence remains stable enough to support interpretation. A profile likelihood examines how distinctly the assumed model can determine a coupling parameter; held-out RMSE examines predictive performance. Together, those measures let the simulation distinguish a well-determined coupling from a relationship that happens to predict well without being uniquely interpretable.
Is the plan to show that crossing always makes the coupling identifiable?

No. The point is to examine when crossing helps, under the assumptions being studied. Its usefulness depends on which donors and batches are connected, what is assumed about batch effects, and whether the anchors retain their intended meaning. A crossed layout provides opportunities for separation; it is not an unconditional guarantee of identifiable biological coupling.
What should the nested layout tell me?

It provides a comparison in which each donor is confined to a batch, so the incidence pattern supplies no within-donor comparison across batches. Under an account that allows separate donor and batch contributions, that creates the donor–batch ambiguity discussed earlier. The simulation can examine how that ambiguity appears in the proposed measure of coupling identifiability, rather than assuming that a prediction score alone will reveal it.
Why vary anchor invariance rather than just compare the two incidence layouts?

Because layout and anchors address different potential sources of ambiguity. Crossing may help distinguish donor from batch, but it cannot by itself ensure that an anchor represents the same cell-state correspondence across the RNA and ATAC measurements. By considering both invariant and non-invariant anchors, the plan can examine whether an apparent benefit of crossing depends on the very correspondence used to align the unpaired modalities.
Would non-invariant anchors necessarily make held-out prediction worse?

Not necessarily. An anchor that fails the intended invariance assumption could undermine a biological interpretation without producing a predictable change in RMSE in every setting. Held-out error measures prediction, while anchor invariance bears on what the alignment means. The simulation should leave room for those outcomes to differ rather than treating prediction error as a direct test of invariance.
What would a profile likelihood contribute that RMSE cannot?

A profile likelihood asks, within the assumed model, how well different values of the coupling quantity can account for the simulated observations after accounting for other allowable quantities. If substantially different coupling values remain comparably compatible, that indicates weak determination of the coupling under that model. RMSE instead asks how close predictions are to held-out responses; multiple couplings could yield similar predictions and therefore similar RMSE.
If the profile likelihood has a distinct optimum, can I conclude that biological coupling has been identified?

Only conditionally. A distinct optimum may indicate that the coupling quantity is well determined within the fitted model and the simulated setting. It does not establish that the assumed batch effects and anchors correctly represent biology. In particular, an assumption that rules out an alternative explanation can make a parameter look well determined even though the data alone do not rule out that explanation.
And if the profile is broad or flat?

That would suggest that a range of coupling values remains compatible with the observations under the profiled model, so the coupling is not sharply determined there. It is a useful way to make ambiguity visible. The interpretation still needs care: the profile concerns the specified coupling quantity and assumptions, not every possible notion of RNA–ATAC coupling.
How do I use held-out RMSE without confusing it with an identifiability measure?

Use it as the predictive counterpart to the profile-likelihood analysis. It can show whether an alignment predicts held-out perturbation responses accurately, while the profile examines whether its coupling quantity is distinguishable within the assumed model. For the broader goal, the relevant predictive comparison is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations. Meeting that target would not, on its own, resolve donor–batch confounding.
Does mentioning unseen donors and perturbations commit this simulation plan to a particular holdout layout?

No particular allocation or implementation is specified here. The plan calls for held-out RMSE, and the broader predictive requirement concerns unseen donors and perturbations. The important distinction at this stage is that held-out observations assess transfer, while crossed versus nested incidence and anchor invariance probe conditions for interpreting the coupling. The plan does not state that any holdout evaluation has already been performed.
Should I expect the profile likelihood and held-out RMSE to agree across the simulated cases?

There is no reason to require agreement. A case might have low held-out RMSE yet a poorly determined coupling quantity, or a distinct profile without achieving the desired held-out predictive improvement. Those are possibilities the two measures can help distinguish, not outcomes that the plan asserts will occur.
How does this simulation plan bear on the question of complete donor nesting making separation impossible?

The nested layout lets you examine the lack of donor-across-batch contrasts directly. Under assumptions that leave donor and batch contributions free to trade off, the incidence pattern cannot uniquely assign their contributions; profiling can make the corresponding ambiguity explicit if it affects the coupling quantity being examined. A predictive result should be reported separately, because held-out RMSE cannot turn an intrinsically confounded incidence pattern into an identifiable one.
So the plan is comparative, not a claim about what the comparison will find?

Exactly. It proposes simulating crossed and nested donor–batch layouts, varying anchor invariance, and assessing both profile likelihood and held-out RMSE. Its purpose is to learn under which stated conditions RNA–ATAC coupling is distinguishable and under which it remains ambiguous, while separately checking predictive transfer. It does not presuppose a particular profile shape, RMSE reduction, or biological conclusion.

I’m simulating six donors across three batches, using crossed or nested donor–batch layouts and anchor shifts from 0% to 20%. I’ll measure coupling-profile curvature and holdout RMSE. What does this activity let me examine?

It lets you examine two different consequences of changing the donor–batch layout and the stability of the shared cell-state anchors. Coupling-profile curvature concerns how sharply the simulated observations distinguish values of the RNA–ATAC coupling quantity under the assumed model. Holdout RMSE concerns predictive error. Comparing them across crossed and nested layouts and across the 0–20% anchor-shift range can reveal whether apparent predictive usefulness tracks, or diverges from, how well the coupling is determined. The activity does not yet state any outcome.
Why keep the number of donors and batches the same for the crossed and nested layouts?

Using six donors and three batches in both layouts makes the incidence pattern the salient contrast in this simulation: the distinction is whether observations cross batch boundaries for donors or keep each donor nested within a batch. The numbers alone do not specify which donor appears in which batch, so they should not be taken to imply a particular allocation or degree of crossing.
Could a design be called crossed if only some donors appear in more than one batch?

Yes, crossing refers to donor–batch overlap rather than a requirement that every donor appear in every batch. For interpreting the result, though, it matters which parts of the three-batch layout that overlap actually connects. Simply labeling a layout “crossed” does not guarantee that every donor and batch contrast relevant to the coupling is supported.
And nested means no donor crosses batches?

That is the pertinent distinction here: in a completely nested layout, each donor is confined to one batch. With six donors and three batches, nesting does not itself say how the donors are distributed among those batches. Its important consequence for the question is the absence of within-donor comparisons across batches.
What does changing the anchor shifts from 0% to 20% add to that comparison?

It gives you a range over which to examine sensitivity to changes in the anchors used for the unpaired RNA–ATAC alignment. The 0% end represents no imposed anchor shift in the simulation; the 20% end represents the upper end of the specified shift range. The activity does not define a particular shift mechanism or intermediate increments, so those should not be inferred from the range alone.
Should I describe 0% anchor shift as proof that the anchors are invariant?

Only within the intended simulation condition: 0% means no shift has been imposed under whatever anchor-shift definition the simulation uses. It is not proof that anchors in actual unpaired measurements are invariant, nor does it independently establish a unique biological correspondence. It provides a reference condition for examining what changes as imposed shifts increase.
How does coupling-profile curvature relate to identifiability?

A profile that changes sharply around a coupling value indicates that, within the assumed model and simulated observations, nearby alternative values fit less similarly. A relatively flat profile indicates less ability to distinguish coupling values. Curvature is therefore a way to quantify local sharpness of the profile, but interpreting it as biological identifiability still depends on whether the model’s assumptions—including those concerning batch effects and anchors—are appropriate.
Does a high curvature mean the donor and batch effects have been separated?

Not automatically. It says something about the profile of the particular coupling quantity being measured. A sharp profile could arise under assumptions that constrain donor or batch effects without the incidence pattern independently separating them. The nested layout still lacks donor-across-batch contrasts, so profile curvature should be read alongside the donor–batch design and the assumptions used to construct the profile.
Then why measure holdout RMSE as well?

Because a well-determined coupling quantity and a useful predictor are not the same thing. Holdout RMSE tests how accurately perturbation responses are predicted for observations kept out of fitting; curvature asks how distinctly the coupling quantity is determined within the model. Measuring both avoids treating a sharp profile as a performance result, or a low prediction error as proof that biological coupling has been identified.
Does this activity itself specify which observations are held out?

No. It specifies holdout RMSE as a measurement, not an exact holdout allocation. For the broader transferable-prediction goal, the relevant condition is unseen donors and perturbations, and the performance target is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models. This activity states neither a particular holdout assignment nor a result against that target.
If holdout RMSE looks good in the nested layout, what could I say?

You could describe the predictive performance under the specified holdout conditions, once measured. You should not infer from it that donor and batch contributions have become distinguishable in a completely nested layout. Predictive accuracy can coexist with donor–batch ambiguity, and the activity has not supplied a result in either direction.
What if curvature changes as anchor shifts increase, but RMSE does not change in the same way?

That would illustrate why the two measurements are kept separate: changes in how sharply coupling is determined need not mirror changes in predictive error. The specific pattern, if any, is something the simulation is meant to measure, not something specified in advance. Nor would a divergence by itself identify the biological cause of an anchor-related change.
Could the reverse happen—RMSE changes while profile curvature stays similar?

It is conceptually possible. Curvature and RMSE answer different questions, so neither is guaranteed to move with the other as the donor–batch layout or anchor shift changes. Reporting them separately would preserve that distinction without assuming which combination the simulation will produce.
What does the comparison of crossed and nested layouts tell me specifically about the earlier identifiability hypothesis?

It provides a way to examine its incidence-pattern component under the simulation’s assumptions. Crossing supplies potential donor-across-batch comparisons; complete nesting does not. Looking at coupling-profile curvature across those layouts and across the anchor-shift range can show how distinctly the coupling quantity is determined in each simulated condition. It would still be necessary to state the assumptions behind the profile before interpreting that distinction as biological RNA–ATAC coupling rather than an effect of the model’s restrictions.
Is six donors across three batches enough, by itself, to settle that question?

No. Those counts define the scale of this activity, not identifiability on their own. The incidence pattern, the anchor behavior, and the assumptions governing batch effects all matter. Two layouts with six donors and three batches can offer different information about donor versus batch simply because their observations connect donors and batches differently.
How should I avoid overstating what the 0–20% range establishes?

Describe it as the imposed range of anchor shifts examined in this simulation. It does not establish that actual anchors shift by any particular percentage, that 20% is a meaningful boundary outside the simulation, or that an outcome at one shift level must persist at others. Its role is to let you measure how the coupling profile and holdout RMSE behave as anchor stability is varied within that specified range.
So I can keep the immediate description quite concrete without claiming that the simulation has already answered the question?

Yes: the activity is to simulate six donors across three batches in crossed or nested donor–batch layouts, impose anchor shifts ranging from 0% to 20%, and measure coupling-profile curvature and holdout RMSE. Those measurements are intended to examine identifiability and prediction as distinct properties. No profile shape, RMSE value, or conclusion about which conditions identify coupling is specified yet.
With invariant anchors, normalized coupling-profile curvature was 0.42 in the crossed designs versus <0.01 in the nested designs. What can I conclude from that comparison?

The coupling profile was substantially sharper in the crossed designs than in the nested designs under the invariant-anchor condition. A normalized curvature of 0.42 indicates more local distinction among coupling values than a curvature below 0.01, assuming the same curvature definition was used for both. That is a comparison of how the coupling quantity is determined within the profiling setup, not a result about holdout RMSE or a standalone proof of biological coupling.
When you say the nested profile is flatter, are you treating <0.01 as zero?

No. The reported value is strictly below 0.01; it is not reported as zero. Calling it comparatively flat describes its small curvature relative to 0.42. It would overstate the number to say that the nested profile has exactly no curvature.
Does the comparison mean the crossed designs identify the coupling?

It shows that, with invariant anchors, the coupling profile is much more sharply curved in the crossed designs than in the nested designs. Whether that amounts to identification requires the assumptions defining the profile and the scope of the coupling quantity to be stated. Curvature alone does not establish that the anchors are biologically valid or that every alternative explanation has been excluded.

Because the reported comparison is conditional on invariant anchors. It describes what the profiles looked like when the anchors were treated as stable correspondences for the RNA–ATAC alignment. Can I say the result holds from 0% through 20% anchor shift?

Is normalized coupling-profile curvature itself a prediction metric?

No. It describes the local shape of the profile for the coupling quantity under the assumed model: a sharper profile distinguishes nearby coupling values more strongly than a flatter one. Prediction would be assessed separately with holdout RMSE. This result contains no holdout RMSE values.
Then it does not tell me whether the 15% RMSE reduction versus RNA-only models was achieved?

Correct. The 0.42 versus <0.01 comparison concerns coupling-profile curvature, not perturbation-response error. It cannot establish whether RMSE was reduced by 15% versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations.
Could I convert 0.42 and <0.01 into a percentage improvement?

It is better to report them in their stated units as normalized curvature. They are not RMSE values, and the nested figure is only an upper bound, not an exact number. Describing their contrast as the 15% predictive improvement would conflate two different quantities.
Does a sharper profile necessarily mean the estimated coupling is correct?

No. A sharp profile means the assumed model more strongly favors a narrower range of coupling values locally. The result is informative about determination within the profiling setup, with that qualification.

No. A flat coupling profile and predictive performance answer different questions. Predictions might be assessed even when the coupling quantity is poorly distinguished, but no prediction outcome is reported here. The nested curvature value should not be turned into a claim about holdout RMSE.
Can I describe the numerical contrast without making an identifiability claim at all?

Yes. You can state: “With invariant anchors, normalized coupling-profile curvature was 0.42 in crossed designs and <0.01 in nested designs.” You could add that the coupling profile was markedly sharper in the crossed designs under that condition. That accurately describes the observation without claiming more than the measurement supplies.

Make clear that the inference concerns the coupling quantity within the assumed profiling model and the invariant-anchor condition. For the nested designs in particular, “<0.01” should be described as very low curvature, not exact mathematical non-identifiability solely on the basis of that number.
How would you express the finding in one careful sentence?

With invariant anchors, the normalized coupling profile was much sharper in crossed donor–batch designs (curvature 0.42) than in nested designs (curvature <0.01), indicating greater local determination of the coupling quantity in the crossed designs under the profiling assumptions, without establishing a holdout-RMSE result.
I’ve decided to restrict identifiable-coupling claims to crossed donor–batch designs with invariant anchors, and to flag nested layouts as nonidentifiable. How should I state that boundary?

State it as a scope rule for interpretation: make identifiable RNA–ATAC coupling claims only when the donor–batch design is crossed and the shared cell-state anchors are invariant. What should I say if the layout is crossed but I cannot establish anchor invariance?

Do not make an identifiable-coupling claim under this decision. And what exactly am I flagging in a nested layout?

Flag the coupling as nonidentifiable under the nested donor–batch layout. The flag warns that the layout does not provide the donor-across-batch contrasts needed to distinguish donor-associated from batch-associated variation for this interpretation. It is a statement about the limits of attributing the inferred RNA–ATAC relationship uniquely, not a claim that no relationship can be fitted or used for prediction.
Would it be accurate to say a nested layout has no biological signal?

No. Nonidentifiable does not mean biologically absent. It means the information available under that layout does not support uniquely separating the biological coupling claim from the relevant donor–batch ambiguity. A biological signal could be present without being distinguishable on that basis.
Does a nested-layout flag invalidate its holdout RMSE?

No. Holdout RMSE measures predictive error; the nonidentifiability flag limits how the fitted relationship can be interpreted. Both can be reported without turning predictive performance into evidence that the donor–batch ambiguity has been resolved.
Should I describe crossed designs as identifiable even if the model allows unrestricted batch effects?

The decision should not be stretched that far. It limits identifiable-coupling claims to crossed designs with invariant anchors, but a claim also needs assumptions under which batch effects can actually be distinguished from coupling. If batch effects can freely mimic the coupling of interest, crossing and invariant anchors alone need not identify it.
Is the decision about separating donor from batch, or about RNA–ATAC coupling itself?

It is a boundary for claims that RNA–ATAC coupling is identifiable. Donor–batch structure matters because ambiguity between donor and batch can undermine that interpretation. Crossing and invariant anchors address different parts of the argument, so neither condition should be described as a substitute for the other.
How strong should the word “nonidentifiable” be for nested layouts?

Use it for the separation at issue: in nested layouts, donor and batch cannot be independently distinguished from the incidence pattern for the intended coupling interpretation. It need not mean that every possible parameter under every stronger assumption is impossible to estimate. The flag should make the limitation clear without implying that all prediction or analysis is impossible.
Should this decision be phrased as achieving the predictive target too?

No. It sets an interpretive boundary for identifiable-coupling claims. The separate predictive target is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations. Restricting claims to crossed designs with invariant anchors does not itself establish that RMSE reduction.
Could I write a short rule that a reader could apply to any design under discussion?

Yes: “Restrict claims of identifiable RNA–ATAC coupling to crossed donor–batch designs with invariant shared cell-state anchors, subject to the stated separation assumptions; flag nested donor–batch layouts as nonidentifiable for that coupling claim.” That preserves the boundary without equating an eligibility condition with proof in every crossed design.
If someone sees an apparent RNA–ATAC alignment in a nested layout, how should the flag affect their reading of it?

They may describe the apparent alignment as an estimated relationship, but should not present it as uniquely identified biological coupling. The flag tells them that donor–batch ambiguity remains for that interpretation. It does not prescribe discarding the alignment or assert a result about its predictive usefulness.
So the decision controls the strength of the interpretation, not whether an alignment can be attempted?

Exactly. It restricts identifiable-coupling claims to crossed designs with invariant anchors and labels nested layouts nonidentifiable. It does not prohibit fitting a relationship or assessing predictions; it prevents those activities from being mistaken for a resolution of the stated identifiability problem.

I want to frame the hypothesis this way: identifying RNA–ATAC coupling requires crossed donor–batch observations and full-rank, matched cell-state anchors. Identical anchors or nested donor–batch designs preclude separation. Can you unpack the two requirements?

They address different ambiguities. Crossed donor–batch observations provide comparisons that can distinguish donor-associated from batch-associated variation. Full-rank, matched cell-state anchors provide distinct, corresponding information for relating the unpaired RNA and ATAC measurements. The hypothesis says both are required: donor–batch crossing cannot supply distinctions missing from the anchors, and informative anchors cannot supply donor-across-batch comparisons missing from a nested design.
What does “matched” mean when the RNA and ATAC measurements are unpaired?

It means the anchors are taken to represent corresponding cell states across the modalities. It does not mean RNA and ATAC were measured together in an observed pair. Because the measurements are unpaired, the validity of that correspondence remains part of what an identifiable-coupling claim must rely on.
Is matching the anchors enough to make them full-rank?

No. Matching concerns whether anchors correspond across RNA and ATAC; full rank concerns whether they provide independent distinctions needed to determine the coupling. Anchors could correspond perfectly yet provide redundant information. The hypothesis requires both a defensible match and sufficient independent information.
Can you explain “full-rank” without specifying a particular model matrix?

In this hypothesis, it means the anchors supply enough independent contrasts for the coupling distinctions one intends to make. If one anchor contributes no distinguishable information beyond another, the relevant anchor information is rank-deficient. The exact mathematical rank condition would depend on how coupling and anchors are represented; the hypothesis does not specify that representation.
Why do identical anchors preclude separation?

Identical anchors do not distinguish the states they are supposed to use as separate reference points. If the proposed separation relies on contrasts between those anchors, their identical information cannot determine which coupling relationship accounts for those contrasts. That is the anchor-side failure described by the hypothesis, distinct from donor–batch confounding.
Should I interpret “identical anchors” as meaning every feature in both modalities must be identical?

The hypothesis does not define identity at that level of detail. The relevant issue is whether the anchors are identical for the information needed to distinguish the coupling. It would be too specific to assert, without further definition, that every RNA and ATAC measurement must be identical. The claim is that anchors that provide no independent coupling-relevant contrast preclude the proposed separation.
What is the corresponding failure in a nested donor–batch design?

When each donor is confined to one batch, the design lacks a comparison of that donor across batches. Donor-associated and batch-associated contributions can then remain confounded by the incidence pattern. Full-rank matched anchors do not create those missing donor–batch observations, so they cannot alone resolve that separation.
If the donor–batch layout is crossed, can I skip checking anchor rank?

No. Crossing addresses the donor–batch side of the problem, not whether the shared anchors distinguish RNA–ATAC coupling. Under this hypothesis, a crossed layout with identical or otherwise rank-deficient anchors still fails the anchor requirement.
And if the anchors are full-rank and matched, can I skip checking the layout?

No. Those anchors can provide the proposed cross-modality distinctions, but they do not tell you how to apportion variation between donor and batch when donors are nested. The two requirements are complementary, not interchangeable.
Does the hypothesis say crossing and full-rank matching are sufficient to prove biological coupling?

It states them as requirements for coupling separation, not as an unconditional proof from those labels alone. A biological interpretation still depends on the assumptions under which batch variation and the anchor correspondences can be distinguished from coupling. In particular, calling a layout crossed or anchors full-rank should not substitute for specifying what those properties distinguish in the coupling claim.
How should I phrase the word “requires” so it is not mistaken for a result already demonstrated?

Keep the statement explicitly hypothetical: “We hypothesize that separating RNA–ATAC coupling requires crossed donor–batch observations together with full-rank, matched cell-state anchors.” Then state the predicted failure cases: identical anchors cannot supply the required anchor distinctions, and nested designs cannot supply the required donor–batch distinctions. This presents a claim to examine, not a completed identification result.
Does this hypothesis concern predictive RMSE as well?

Its direct claim concerns identifiability: whether coupling can be separated from the relevant ambiguities. It does not predict a particular held-out perturbation RMSE. The separate performance requirement remains a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations; meeting that requirement would not, by itself, establish the anchor and incidence conditions.
Could an identical-anchor case still produce useful predictions?

The hypothesis does not rule that out. It says identical anchors preclude the specified separation of coupling, not that all fitted relationships or predictions must fail. Predictive usefulness and the ability to attribute a relationship uniquely to biological RNA–ATAC coupling remain different questions.
Is the same distinction important for nested designs?

Yes. Calling a nested design nonseparating does not assert that it contains no biological information or cannot yield a prediction. It means the nested donor–batch incidence pattern cannot provide the contrasts required to distinguish donor from batch for the coupling interpretation at issue.
Can you give me a compact statement that keeps the two ways separation can fail distinct?

“We hypothesize that identifiable RNA–ATAC coupling requires both crossed donor–batch observations and full-rank, matched cell-state anchors: nested designs confound donor with batch, while identical anchors lack the independent cross-modality distinctions needed for coupling separation.”
At what anchor rank and donor–batch overlap does unpaired ATAC lower joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE by at least 15%?

That is an empirical threshold question; no rank or overlap threshold is specified yet. The outcome to examine is perturbation-response RMSE on holdouts where both the donor and perturbation are unseen, compared with an RNA-only model under the same holdout conditions. Anchor rank and donor–batch overlap describe different conditions that might affect whether unpaired ATAC contributes transferable information.
What does “joint donor–perturbation holdout” require me to keep distinct from other holdouts?

It asks about predictions under the combined unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation condition. A result for an unseen donor with a familiar perturbation, or an unseen perturbation in a familiar donor, would not by itself answer the joint question. Likewise, an aggregate RMSE that mixes those conditions would need to identify the joint subset before it could establish this threshold.
How should I read “at least 15%” in this question?

Against the RNA-only comparison, the RMSE with unpaired ATAC would have to be no greater than 85% of the RNA-only RMSE on the same joint holdout. Equality at a 15% reduction meets “at least 15%.” This is a relative comparison, not a requirement to reduce RMSE by 15 absolute units.
Is there already an anchor-rank value that answers the question?

No value is supplied here. “Full-rank” also does not specify a universal numeric rank: rank is defined relative to the coupling distinctions represented by the anchors. The question asks at what degree of independent anchor information the predictive threshold is reached, which cannot be inferred solely from the word “full-rank.”
Could simply adding more anchors answer it?

Not on its own. A count of anchors is different from their rank: additional anchors may repeat information already present. Nor does higher rank automatically imply a 15% RMSE reduction. Rank bears on whether the proposed RNA–ATAC correspondence contains distinguishable information; the holdout comparison determines whether that information improves prediction by the specified amount.
What does donor–batch overlap contribute to this threshold question?

Overlap describes whether donors are observed across batch contexts in a way that permits donor and batch variation to be distinguished under the relevant assumptions. Its possible predictive contribution is to reduce reliance on relationships that track a particular donor–batch arrangement rather than transferring to unseen donors. How much overlap is enough for a ≥15% RMSE reduction is not given; it must be distinguished from the separate question of whether an incidence pattern supports an identifiability claim.
Can I measure overlap just by counting donors that cross batches?

That count could describe one aspect of overlap, but it would not necessarily capture which batches are connected by those donors. The placement of the overlaps matters as well as their number. This question does not prescribe an overlap metric, so a numeric answer would need to make clear what measure of overlap it uses.
Would a connected donor–batch pattern guarantee the 15% improvement?

No. Connectivity can be relevant to distinguishing relative donor and batch contributions under stated assumptions, but it is not a guarantee that unpaired ATAC lowers joint-holdout prediction error. The ≥15% requirement is a performance result that must be established by the RMSE comparison, not deduced from incidence alone.
Would full-rank matched anchors guarantee it instead?

No. Full-rank, matched anchors may be necessary for a particular identifiable-coupling claim, but the predictive target is distinct. Even an alignment whose coupling quantity can be distinguished under its assumptions might fail to improve joint-holdout RMSE by at least 15%. Conversely, a predictive improvement would not by itself prove the coupling biologically identifiable.
How should I think about rank and overlap together rather than as two independent cutoffs?

Ask which combinations of anchor rank and donor–batch overlap, if any, reach the RMSE threshold on joint donor–perturbation holdouts. A rank threshold found under one incidence pattern need not apply under another, and an overlap threshold found with informative anchors need not apply with redundant anchors. The question leaves their interaction open rather than asserting that either variable has a standalone cutoff.
Does the question imply that improvement increases steadily with rank or overlap?

No. It asks where a threshold is reached, not whether RMSE changes monotonically as either condition increases. A steady trend, a discontinuity, or no qualifying combination would all require observed results; none is specified here.
If several combinations meet the threshold, what would “at what rank and overlap” mean?

It would call for reporting the qualifying combinations using clearly defined rank and overlap measures, rather than collapsing them into one unsupported universal cutoff. If a minimal qualifying combination can be established within a stated set of conditions, it should be described as conditional on those conditions. The question does not presuppose that there is a unique minimum.
And if no combination meets a 15% reduction?

Then the answer would be that no examined combination reaches the ≥15% reduction on the specified joint holdout, within whatever conditions were examined. That is a possible answer to the question, not a result given here; it would not justify a broader claim about every possible anchor or donor–batch design.
Can the coupling-profile curvature values answer this threshold question?

No. Curvature describes how sharply a coupling quantity is determined within a profiling setup; the threshold is stated in joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE relative to RNA-only prediction. One cannot convert a curvature value into a ≥15% RMSE reduction. The predictive comparison has to be read from RMSE results for the relevant holdout.
What would be the most careful short statement of the question?

“For which defined combinations of anchor rank and donor–batch overlap, if any, does adding unpaired ATAC reduce perturbation-response RMSE by at least 15% versus RNA-only prediction on joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdouts?” It states the comparison and conditions while leaving the threshold location open.
I’m grid-searching DonorBatchSim v1 across anchor ranks 1–4 and 0–3 cross-batch donors, comparing RNA–ATAC with RNA-only unseen-donor/perturbation RMSE. How does that address the threshold question?

The grid examines combinations of two conditions rather than assuming either has a universal cutoff. Anchor rank varies the independent information available from the anchors; the number of cross-batch donors varies one measure of donor–batch overlap. At each combination, the relevant outcome is whether RNA–ATAC reduces perturbation-response RMSE by at least 15% versus RNA-only prediction on the unseen-donor/perturbation holdout. The activity specifies the comparison, not its results.
Does 1–4 mean four anchor-rank settings, and 0–3 mean four overlap settings?

Read as integer settings, yes: ranks 1, 2, 3, and 4, crossed with 0, 1, 2, and 3 cross-batch donors. That describes 16 rank-by-overlap combinations in the grid. It does not say how many DonorBatchSim v1 instances contribute to a combination or what any combination’s RMSE will be.
What exactly is being counted by “cross-batch donors”?

It counts donors observed across batches, rather than the number of batches or the number of anchor correspondences. A setting of 0 has no donor crossing batches; a setting of 3 has three such donors. The count alone does not specify which batches those donors connect, so it is a limited description of the overlap pattern.
Could two designs both have two cross-batch donors but different implications?

Yes. The two donors might connect different parts of the donor–batch incidence pattern. Thus a count of two does not, by itself, guarantee the same donor–batch contrasts in every layout. If the grid yields different outcomes at the same count, the count should not be presented as a complete description of overlap.
And anchor rank is not just another way of saying how many anchors there are?

Correct. Rank concerns independent anchor information relevant to distinguishing the coupling, whereas an anchor count can include redundancy. The settings 1–4 specify ranks for this grid; they do not, on their own, state the number of anchors or establish that rank 4 is sufficient for every coupling interpretation.
What is the point of crossing every rank setting with every cross-batch-donor setting?

It allows the RMSE comparison to be examined at each combination. You can ask whether a given anchor rank qualifies only with particular donor–batch overlap, or whether a particular overlap count qualifies only with particular rank. The grid does not assume that improving one condition compensates for a limitation in the other.
How should the RNA–ATAC versus RNA-only comparison be made conceptually?

The two RMSE values need to concern the same unseen-donor/perturbation prediction condition, because the question is whether adding unpaired ATAC improves on RNA-only prediction there. Comparing RNA–ATAC error on one kind of holdout with RNA-only error on another would not isolate the stated difference. No RMSE values or comparison outcomes are supplied in the activity.
Does “unseen-donor/perturbation” mean both have to be unseen together?

Yes, for the joint donor–perturbation threshold question being addressed. An unseen donor with an already-seen perturbation, or an unseen perturbation with an already-seen donor, is a different transfer condition. The grid’s RMSE comparison should be interpreted for the joint condition stated here.
What calculation determines whether a grid combination clears the 15% threshold?

Its RNA–ATAC perturbation-response RMSE must be at most 0.85 times the RNA-only RMSE on the corresponding unseen-donor/perturbation holdout. That expresses a reduction of at least 15% relative to RNA-only. The activity does not provide either RMSE, so it does not yet identify a qualifying combination.
If rank 4 with three cross-batch donors qualifies, can I call that the threshold?

Not on that observation alone. A qualifying combination shows that the target is reached at that combination; identifying a threshold would also require examining the other grid combinations and defining what “threshold” means when rank and overlap can vary together. The proposed grid makes those comparisons possible but states no qualifying result.
What if a lower rank qualifies at a higher overlap count, while a higher rank qualifies at a lower count?

Then a single cutoff for anchor rank or cross-batch donors would not capture the answer. The careful description would identify the qualifying rank-and-overlap combinations within this grid. Your example is a possible interpretation pattern, not an outcome reported for DonorBatchSim v1.
Should I assume RMSE improves monotonically from rank 1 to 4?

No. Ordering the rank settings does not establish an ordering of predictive performance. The grid search asks how RNA–ATAC versus RNA-only holdout RMSE behaves across those settings; monotonic improvement would be a finding to establish, not a premise of the activity.
Does increasing the count from zero to three cross-batch donors necessarily produce a steadier improvement?

No. The count changes one aspect of donor–batch overlap, but neither the placement of that overlap nor its effect on prediction is specified by the count alone. The grid may reveal a pattern, but this activity does not state one.
Is the zero-cross-batch-donor setting useful even though it has no crossing donors?

It is part of the specified comparison range and represents the absence of donor-across-batch overlap by that measure. It lets the grid include that condition alongside settings with one, two, or three cross-batch donors. Its predictive RMSE still has to be measured; a lack of crossing does not, by itself, give an RMSE value.
If RNA–ATAC predicts well at zero cross-batch donors, would that make donor and batch separable?

No. Predictive performance and donor–batch separation are different claims. A favorable RMSE comparison in a setting with no cross-batch donors would not create the missing donor-across-batch observations or, by itself, establish identifiable biological RNA–ATAC coupling.
Likewise, does a high anchor rank establish the 15% predictive gain?

No. Rank describes the independent information represented by the anchors for the intended coupling distinction. The ≥15% criterion is determined by the RNA–ATAC versus RNA-only RMSE comparison on the joint holdout. Neither rank nor overlap can be substituted for that observed predictive comparison.
Are coupling-profile curvature plots the outcome of this grid search?

Not the stated outcome for this activity. DonorBatchSim v1 contains coupling-profile curvature plots, but this grid search specifies a comparison of RNA–ATAC and RNA-only unseen-donor/perturbation RMSE. Curvature can bear on how distinctly coupling is determined; it cannot be read as the percentage reduction in held-out RMSE.
Does this grid by itself test whether the anchors are matched or invariant?

It specifies anchor ranks 1–4, not a variation in anchor matching or invariance. Those properties matter to interpreting a biological coupling claim, but they should not be described as additional axes of this grid search unless explicitly specified. The immediate question here is where, across the stated rank and cross-batch-donor settings, the predictive RMSE comparison reaches the target.
What if no setting in the grid reaches a 15% reduction?

That would answer the question only within the examined settings: none of the anchor ranks 1–4 paired with 0–3 cross-batch donors would have reached the ≥15% reduction under the evaluated holdout comparison. It would not establish that unpaired ATAC can never reach the target under other conditions. No such outcome is reported here.
Can I describe the grid as finding the minimum rank and overlap already?

Not yet. Grid-searching supplies a way to compare the specified combinations; it does not state which, if any, qualify. Even after RMSE values are available, a single “minimum rank and overlap” would require care if multiple combinations trade one condition against the other.
Give me a concise description of the activity without implying a threshold has been found.

“Grid-search DonorBatchSim v1 over anchor ranks 1–4 and 0–3 cross-batch donors, comparing RNA–ATAC with RNA-only perturbation-response RMSE on joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdouts to determine which combinations, if any, achieve a reduction of at least 15%.”
AnchorOverlapGrid v1 reports anchor rank, cross-batch donor overlap, joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE, and improvement versus RNA-only. How should I describe what this artifact makes available?

Describe it as a record of the predictive comparison across anchor-rank and donor–batch-overlap conditions. It reports the conditions, the RMSE on the joint holdout, and the improvement relative to RNA-only prediction. That makes it relevant to asking where unpaired RNA–ATAC prediction reaches the ≥15% RMSE-reduction target. The artifact description does not supply any particular values or say which conditions, if any, reach that target.
Why report both joint holdout RMSE and improvement versus RNA-only?

They answer related but different questions. RMSE states the predictive error under the joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation condition. Improvement versus RNA-only states how the RNA–ATAC prediction compares with the specified baseline. An RMSE value alone does not tell you the relative gain without the comparable RNA-only error; an improvement figure alone does not convey the reported RMSE.
What should a reader understand by “joint” in that field?

Both the donor and the perturbation are held out for the prediction being evaluated. It is not enough that the donor alone is unseen or that the perturbation alone is unseen. Keeping that condition explicit matters because the 15% requirement concerns transfer on unseen donors and perturbations together.
Does the improvement field necessarily mean a percentage?

The artifact description says “improvement versus RNA-only” but does not specify its units or calculation. To compare that field with a ≥15% target, it would need to represent a relative percentage reduction in RMSE, or provide enough information to calculate one. An absolute difference in RMSE would not by itself be a percentage reduction.
What calculation would correspond to the target if the improvement is expressed as a percentage?

For comparable RMSE values on the same joint holdout, the relative reduction is 100% × (RNA-only RMSE − RNA–ATAC RMSE) / RNA-only RMSE. A value of at least 15% meets the target; equivalently, RNA–ATAC RMSE is at most 0.85 times RNA-only RMSE. That explains how to read a percentage improvement, not a claim that AnchorOverlapGrid v1 reports any particular percentage.
Why must the RNA-only comparison use the same joint holdout?

Otherwise the reported difference could reflect different evaluation conditions rather than the contribution of unpaired ATAC. The question is whether RNA–ATAC lowers perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only for unseen donors and perturbations together. A baseline assessed on a different holdout would not answer that comparison directly.
What does the anchor-rank field tell me that a count of anchors would not?

Rank describes the independent information attributed to the anchors for the coupling distinctions being considered. A count could include anchors that repeat one another. The rank field therefore helps distinguish potentially informative anchor conditions from redundant ones, but it does not alone predict the size of the RMSE improvement or establish that the anchors are correctly matched across RNA and ATAC.
And what is captured by cross-batch donor overlap?

It describes the presence of donors observed across batch contexts, which is relevant to distinguishing donor-associated from batch-associated variation. As reported here, it is a condition to compare against predictive error and improvement. An overlap value alone need not describe every detail of which batches are connected, so it should not automatically be treated as a complete identifiability assessment.
Can I read an anchor-rank and overlap pair as a proven predictive threshold?

Only after inspecting the corresponding improvement on the joint holdout. The condition fields say where a result was evaluated; they do not themselves say that RNA–ATAC improved on RNA-only, much less by at least 15%. The artifact description supplies the reported fields, not their values or an identified threshold.
If several combinations show an improvement of at least 15%, how would I describe that?

You would identify the qualifying rank-and-overlap combinations, using the improvement figures calculated on the joint holdout. Avoid replacing several qualifying combinations with a single universal rank or overlap cutoff unless the reported values support that simplification. That is guidance for interpreting possible entries, not a statement that any entries qualify.
Would a qualifying improvement establish that the RNA–ATAC coupling is biologically identifiable?

No. It would establish the specified predictive comparison for that condition, provided the improvement is a comparable relative RMSE reduction. Biological identifiability is a separate question about whether donor–batch effects and the anchor correspondence can be distinguished from coupling. The rank, overlap, and RMSE fields can inform that discussion, but predictive gain alone cannot settle it.
Could a condition have a reported improvement even if its coupling remains ambiguous?

Yes, in principle. A predictor can benefit from information in unpaired ATAC while the biological interpretation of its alignment remains ambiguous. AnchorOverlapGrid v1 is described as reporting predictive quantities alongside rank and overlap; that does not turn its improvement field into a coupling-profile or identifiability measurement.
Should I say this artifact contains coupling-profile curvature plots too?

Not on the basis of its stated contents. AnchorOverlapGrid v1 is described as reporting anchor rank, cross-batch donor overlap, joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE, and improvement versus RNA-only. Coupling-profile curvature is a different quantity, and it is not listed as a reported field here.
Does the name AnchorOverlapGrid v1 imply anything about other versions?
No. It identifies this artifact; its description does not establish a prior version, a later version, or changes between versions.
What if an improvement entry is positive but less than 15%?

If it represents a relative percentage reduction computed on the comparable joint holdout, a positive value below 15% would mean RNA–ATAC has lower RMSE than RNA-only there but does not reach the ≥15% target. An improvement of exactly 15% would meet it. Those are interpretations of possible values, not reported outcomes from the artifact.
What if the improvement is negative?

Under the relative-reduction calculation, a negative value would mean RNA–ATAC RMSE exceeds RNA-only RMSE on the same joint holdout. Again, the description does not say whether any such value occurs. It is important to check the artifact’s definition of “improvement” before assigning that sign interpretation.
Can you give me one careful description of AnchorOverlapGrid v1?

“AnchorOverlapGrid v1 reports anchor rank and cross-batch donor overlap alongside joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdout RMSE and improvement versus RNA-only. These fields support examination of which evaluated conditions, if any, achieve a relative RMSE reduction of at least 15%, without by themselves establishing biological coupling identifiability.”

AnchorOverlapGrid v1 reports that rank-3 anchors and three cross-batch donors yielded joint donor–perturbation holdout RNA–ATAC RMSE of 0.66, versus 0.80 for RNA-only—a 17.5% reduction. What does this result establish?

For that reported rank-and-overlap combination, RNA–ATAC had lower perturbation-response RMSE than RNA-only on the joint holdout. The absolute RMSE difference is 0.14, and 0.14 divided by the RNA-only RMSE of 0.80 gives the stated 17.5% relative reduction. It is a predictive comparison for this combination, not a determination of the biological meaning of the RNA–ATAC coupling.
Does “joint holdout” mean the result is about a donor and a perturbation that are both unseen?
