It means the batch-exclusive and batch-bridging perturbation conditions are compared with the donor component matched. That helps keep differences in which donors are represented from being confused with differences in perturbation–batch arrangement. It does not mean RNA and ATAC were measured as paired observations for each donor.
Does donor matching make the exclusive and bridging conditions identical except for perturbation placement?

Not from the artifact description alone. It tells us the donors are matched, but does not specify every other feature of the conditions. The comparison should retain its stated scope rather than claiming that all other possible differences have been controlled.
Could you clarify the difference between batch-exclusive and batch-bridging perturbations?

A batch-exclusive perturbation is confined to a batch context; a batch-bridging perturbation is represented across batch contexts. This describes perturbation–batch incidence. It is separate from whether donors appear across batches and separate from whether RNA and ATAC measurements are paired.
Why keep both perturbation arrangements in one artifact?

It lets a reader examine whether the recorded coupling curvature and joint-holdout RMSE differ when perturbations do or do not bridge batches, with the donor comparison matched. Keeping the arrangements together makes the intended contrast clear without presuming which arrangement will have a sharper profile or lower prediction error.
How should I read the 0–20% control-contamination field?

As the stated range of contamination conditions recorded for the controls. The 0% condition indicates no imposed contamination under the artifact’s definition, and 20% is the stated upper end. The description does not specify the intermediate levels or exactly how the percentage of contamination is defined, so it is best not to infer a schedule or mechanism.
Does the range mean curvature or RMSE must change steadily as contamination increases?

No. A range of conditions makes that relationship examinable; it does not establish a monotonic trend, a threshold, or even that either outcome changes. Those would have to come from the recorded measurements, not from the artifact’s list of fields.
What assumption is challenged by contaminating the control peaks?

The relevant concern is whether peaks used as controls remain a useful reference for batch-associated accessibility rather than also carrying biological signal relevant to the interpretation. Contamination challenges that reference. Recording a contamination level does not by itself tell us whether the controls still distinguish batch-driven correlations from target-specific coupling at that level.
Does calling them control peaks mean their behavior is known to be batch-only?

No. Their proposed use as controls depends on that interpretation being appropriate. An artifact that varies control contamination is especially important not to describe as though the controls are guaranteed to remain clean batch-only references throughout the range.
What does the coupling-curvature field report?

It reports the local sharpness of a profile for the coupling quantity under the profiling setup. A sharper profile distinguishes nearby coupling values more strongly than a flatter one. Curvature is not itself the coupling value, and it does not automatically establish that the coupling has a unique biological interpretation.
And what does the joint-holdout RMSE field report?

It reports perturbation-response prediction error for a holdout in which both the donor and perturbation are unseen. It is a predictive measure, not a measure of whether batch effects have been separated from biological coupling. The artifact description does not supply particular RMSE values.
Why record both curvature and RMSE instead of selecting one outcome?

They address different questions. Curvature bears on how distinctly the coupling quantity is determined within an assumed analysis; RMSE bears on transfer of perturbation-response predictions to the joint holdout. One could change without the other, so recording both prevents a predictive result from being mistaken for an identifiability result, or vice versa.
Could lower RMSE demonstrate that the controls successfully separated biology from batch?

No. Lower RMSE, if observed, would describe better prediction under the relevant comparison. It would not prove that the control peaks captured all pertinent batch variation or that the inferred coupling is biological. The separation claim requires its own assumptions and evidence about distinguishable alternatives.
Could high coupling curvature demonstrate that the predictions transfer?
No. A sharp coupling profile does not specify how accurately perturbation responses are predicted for unseen donors and perturbations. The joint-holdout RMSE field addresses that separate question.
Can ControlPeakStress v1, just by recording joint-holdout RMSE, establish the 15% reduction versus RNA-only?

No. The broader target is a reduction of at least 15% in perturbation-response RMSE relative to RNA-only models on the same unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation condition. The stated contents of ControlPeakStress v1 include joint-holdout RMSE, but do not specify an RNA-only comparison or values demonstrating that reduction.
Does donor matching mean the joint holdout is necessarily constructed identically for every entry?

The artifact description does not specify the holdout assignments. Donor matching concerns the comparison of the exclusive and bridging perturbation conditions; it should not be expanded into an unreported claim about exactly which observations are held out in each entry.
What comparisons are reasonable to describe as available in principle?

The recorded fields support examining exclusive versus bridging perturbations under donor-matched conditions, and examining recorded curvature and RMSE across the stated control-contamination range. To interpret a particular difference, one would need to keep track of which condition and outcome are being compared. The artifact description does not specify the resulting differences.
Would it be accurate to say the artifact proves perturbation bridging protects against contaminated controls?

No. It records conditions and outcomes relevant to examining that possibility. The fact that bridging and contamination are both represented does not establish protection, its magnitude, or a causal mechanism. It also does not imply that a control-based adjustment succeeds at every contamination level.
Does the artifact say whether control-peak adjustment is applied or ablated?

Not in its stated contents. It records control contamination, coupling curvature, and joint-holdout RMSE for the donor-matched perturbation arrangements. Contamination of controls and a with-versus-without-adjustment comparison are different things; the latter should not be attributed to ControlPeakStress v1 solely from this description.
Could I present it as evidence for a global alignment between unpaired RNA and ATAC?

Not merely from the artifact description. The curvature field concerns a coupling profile, and the RMSE field concerns held-out prediction. Neither field’s presence establishes a unique global alignment or settles the biological meaning of every RNA–ATAC correspondence.
What is a short description that keeps those limits intact?

“ControlPeakStress v1 records donor-matched batch-exclusive and batch-bridging perturbation conditions across 0–20% control contamination, alongside coupling-profile curvature and joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE. It makes profile sharpness and predictive error available for separate comparison without, by its description alone, establishing an identifiability or RNA-only performance result.”

I’ve decided to allow batch-exclusive perturbations only with verified batch-only controls, and to require batch-bridging perturbations when the controls carry biological signal. How should I state this rule?

State it as a conditional rule for using the perturbation arrangements: batch-exclusive perturbations are allowed only when the control peaks have been verified as batch-only. If the controls carry biological signal, the pertinent perturbations must bridge batches. The rule distinguishes a clean batch reference from one that cannot be interpreted as batch-only; it does not say that either condition, by itself, proves biological target coupling.
What does “verified batch-only” need to convey?

It means more than calling peaks controls. Their use as a batch-only reference must be justified for the interpretation being made: the relevant signal in those peaks must not also be the biological signal one is trying to distinguish from batch. The decision does not specify a verification procedure or a numerical cutoff, so neither should be implied.
If a perturbation appears in only one batch and the controls are merely labeled negative controls, is that enough to allow it?

No. For a batch-exclusive perturbation, the decision requires verified batch-only controls. A label alone does not establish that the controls are free of biological signal relevant to the coupling claim.
What if I simply do not know whether the controls carry biological signal?

Unknown control behavior does not satisfy the requirement for verified batch-only controls, so it does not justify allowing batch-exclusive perturbations under this rule. At the same time, uncertainty is not itself a finding that the controls carry biological signal. Keep those two statements distinct.
Why does biological signal in the controls change what I require of the perturbations?

Controls that carry biological signal cannot serve as an unqualified batch-only reference for separating that signal from batch-associated accessibility. Requiring perturbations to bridge batches supplies a different kind of comparison: the same perturbation is represented across batch contexts. The decision makes that bridge necessary when the controls are biologically contaminated; it does not say the bridge repairs the controls or resolves every remaining ambiguity.
Does a batch bridge mean I need paired RNA and ATAC measurements?

No. Batch-bridging describes perturbation–batch incidence: a perturbation appears across batch contexts. RNA and ATAC can still be unpaired. A bridge supplies a potential perturbation-across-batch contrast, not a matched observation of both modalities.
Could donor crossing substitute for a batch-bridging perturbation when the controls contain biological signal?

Not under this decision. Donor crossing concerns observing donors across batches; perturbation bridging concerns observing the same perturbation across batches. The rule specifically requires the latter when controls carry biological signal, so the presence of donor overlap should not be described as satisfying that requirement.
If controls are verified batch-only, does the rule require perturbations to bridge batches anyway?

It does not impose that requirement in that case. It allows batch-exclusive perturbations when the controls are verified batch-only. “Allows” is important: it means batch exclusivity is permitted under the stated condition, not that the resulting coupling is automatically identifiable or that prediction must improve.
And if the controls carry biological signal but perturbations bridge batches, may I say coupling has been identified?

No. Bridging satisfies the requirement this decision places on that situation, but it is not a guarantee of identifiable coupling. The biological interpretation still depends on whether the available comparisons and assumptions distinguish target-specific coupling from the relevant batch-driven alternatives.
Do biologically contaminated controls become valid batch-only controls once the perturbations bridge batches?

No. The controls still carry biological signal and should not be called verified batch-only controls. Bridging is an additional requirement for the perturbation arrangement in that situation, not a change to the controls’ properties.
Does the rule prohibit analyzing batch-exclusive perturbations if the controls are not verified?

The rule says not to allow batch-exclusive perturbations under its stated criterion without verified batch-only controls. It need not be expanded into a claim that the measurements cannot be examined or that a predictor cannot be fitted. The important limit is not to treat an unverified control reference as satisfying the condition for allowing that batch-exclusive arrangement.
Should I describe this as a rule for every possible use of ATAC?

No. Keep it tied to the decision about batch-exclusive versus batch-bridging perturbations when relying on control peaks to address batch-associated accessibility. It does not declare a universal requirement for every ATAC analysis or specify how all other sources of information must be handled.
What if only some control peaks carry biological signal?

For controls being relied on as a batch-only reference, biological signal is incompatible with describing them as verified batch-only. If the controls used for the relevant comparison carry biological signal, the decision requires batch-bridging perturbations. It does not provide a contamination-percentage threshold or a rule for averaging clean and contaminated controls together.
Does “batch-bridging” mean every perturbation must appear in every batch?

No. The rule requires a bridge for the pertinent perturbations when controls carry biological signal, but it does not specify that every perturbation must occur in every batch or give a minimum number of batches. It would be too strong to infer a fully crossed perturbation–batch design from the word “bridging.”
Is one bridge automatically sufficient, regardless of which batches it connects?

The decision does not say so. A bridge must be relevant to the perturbation and batch contrast at issue. Merely counting a perturbation as batch-bridging does not establish that all pertinent batch-associated alternatives are distinguished.
Could verified batch-only controls eliminate the need to consider donor–batch confounding?

No. Verification addresses the proposed interpretation of the control peaks. It does not, on its own, create donor-across-batch observations or settle how donor-associated and batch-associated variation are separated. Allowing batch-exclusive perturbations under this rule is narrower than declaring the entire RNA–ATAC coupling identifiable.
Does this decision say anything about the size of the predictive improvement?

No. It sets conditions for allowing batch-exclusive perturbations or requiring batch bridges, based on whether controls are verified batch-only or carry biological signal. It supplies no joint-holdout RMSE values and does not establish the separate target of reducing perturbation-response RMSE by 15% versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations.
Can I say that meeting the rule is necessary for the biological interpretation but not sufficient for the RMSE target?

You can say that meeting the applicable condition is required by this decision for the perturbation arrangement being used. Do not turn it into a universal theorem of biological identifiability. It is also not a predictive-performance result: whether the RMSE target is met must be assessed separately.
Give me one sentence that I can apply without conflating the two control conditions.

“Allow batch-exclusive perturbations only when the control peaks used for the comparison are verified to be batch-only; when those controls carry biological signal, require the pertinent perturbations to bridge batches, without treating either condition alone as proof of identifiable coupling or predictive improvement.”
I’d like to propose transporting within-batch RNA perturbation contrasts using unpaired ATAC module scores, donor-overlap weighting, and placebo-batch falsification. How do these pieces fit together?

The within-batch RNA contrasts provide the perturbation-response information to be transported. Unpaired ATAC module scores are proposed as additional information about how that response might carry across contexts, while donor-overlap weighting takes account of how much donor–batch overlap supports a comparison. Placebo-batch falsification challenges the resulting interpretation by asking whether the approach also produces an apparent signal under a batch-based comparison that should not substantiate the intended transfer. Together, they form a proposed approach, not a demonstrated improvement or a guarantee of identifiability.
What do you mean by a within-batch RNA perturbation contrast?

It is a comparison of RNA perturbation responses made within a batch rather than inferred solely from differences between batches. Keeping the comparison within a batch can avoid treating a simple between-batch difference as the perturbation response. It does not automatically eliminate other sources of confounding or show that the contrast will transfer to another donor or perturbation.
Why transport the contrast instead of treating it as the final response prediction?

A contrast observed within one context is not, by itself, a prediction for an unseen context. “Transport” expresses the proposed step of using that RNA-based contrast to inform perturbation-response predictions beyond where it was observed. Whether it transports accurately is an open predictive question, especially under donor–batch confounding.
Does transporting a contrast mean I assume the response is identical across donors?

No. Transporting a response need not mean asserting identical responses for all donors. It does require some defensible basis for using the observed contrast when predicting outside its original context. The proposal names unpaired ATAC module scores and donor-overlap weighting as possible aids, but does not state a particular rule for how donor differences are represented.
How are unpaired ATAC module scores supposed to help if RNA and ATAC were not measured together?

They are proposed as accessibility-derived information that could guide the transport of the RNA contrasts without requiring an observed RNA–ATAC pair for each unit. That use still depends on a justified relationship between the scores and the RNA perturbation responses. Because the measurements are unpaired, a useful score does not automatically reveal a uniquely identified biological correspondence.
Does “module score” specify which accessibility features are combined or how?

No. The proposal names ATAC module scores but does not define the modules, scoring calculation, or how the scores enter a predictor. It is accurate to describe their intended role as accessibility-based information for transport, without supplying an unprovided construction.
Should I describe the module scores as measurements of each RNA perturbation response?

That would be too strong. They are derived from the unpaired ATAC measurements, not direct paired measurements of an RNA response. Their proposed value is whether they contain information that improves transport; the relationship between a score and a particular RNA contrast remains something to justify and evaluate.
What does donor-overlap weighting contribute?

It proposes taking the degree of donor overlap across batch contexts into account when relying on the available contrasts and ATAC information. Overlap can matter because comparisons supported by donors appearing across batches offer different information about donor and batch variation from comparisons without that overlap. Weighting does not create missing comparisons, and the proposal does not prescribe a weighting formula.
Is donor-overlap weighting the same as batch correction?

Not necessarily. Weighting addresses how donor-overlap information influences transport; batch correction would refer to a particular way of accounting for batch-associated measurements. The proposal does not specify either an explicit batch-effect model or a correction procedure, so it should not be described as having removed batch effects merely because it uses donor-overlap weights.
If donors are completely nested in batches, could weighting solve that?

Weighting cannot manufacture an observation of the same donor across batches. With complete nesting, unrestricted donor and batch contributions cannot be separated from incidence alone. A transported predictor might still be evaluated under additional assumptions, but a donor-overlap weight cannot, by itself, make a missing donor–batch contrast identifiable.
Would simply having some donor overlap make the transport valid?

No. The overlap needs to support the comparisons relevant to the intended transfer, and the relationship between ATAC module scores and RNA contrasts must also hold where predictions are made. Donor overlap is information for the approach, not a stand-alone validation of the transported response or its biological interpretation.
Why include a placebo-batch falsification step?

It is a proposed challenge to the interpretation that the transported signal reflects a transferable perturbation response rather than batch structure. A placebo-batch check asks whether a batch-based contrast, treated as though it supported the intended signal, produces a result that would be troubling for that interpretation. The proposal does not specify how placebo batches are defined or report the outcome of such a check.
What does the word “falsification” imply here? Would passing the placebo check prove the approach works?

No. Falsification means setting up a check that can expose a particular weakness. A concerning placebo-batch result could undermine the proposed interpretation, but a reassuring result would only address the batch-related alternatives that the check is capable of detecting. It would not prove that all batch effects are absent, that RNA–ATAC coupling is biologically identified, or that predictions meet the RMSE target.
Can the placebo-batch check substitute for donor overlap?

No. It can test for a misleading batch-related pattern under its chosen comparison; it does not add donor-across-batch observations. Donor-overlap weighting and placebo-batch falsification therefore serve different purposes: one uses available overlap to inform transport, and the other probes whether a batch-based alternative might produce an apparent result.
Does making the RNA contrast within a batch eliminate the need for the placebo check?

Not necessarily. A within-batch contrast limits one straightforward source of between-batch confusion, but transporting that contrast using information from other contexts can still be vulnerable to donor–batch structure. The placebo-batch check remains a proposed way to challenge the transported interpretation rather than assuming the within-batch starting point settles it.
Could the ATAC module scores predict well because they track batch rather than transferable biology?

That is a possibility the proposal needs to distinguish. A batch-associated score could appear informative in some comparisons without representing a transferable relationship between accessibility and RNA perturbation response. Donor-overlap information and placebo-batch falsification may help probe that alternative, but neither guarantees it has been excluded.
If a placebo-batch check raises a warning, does that show the ATAC scores contain no biological information?

No. A warning would suggest that the intended interpretation is not cleanly distinguished from the batch-based alternative tested. It would not establish that the scores lack all biological information or that every transported prediction must fail. The scope of the warning should match the particular falsification comparison.
What if the placebo check looks reassuring but the prediction RMSE is poor?

Then the check would not supply the missing predictive performance. It could indicate that a particular batch-based alternative was not detected while the transported predictions still have high error. Placebo-batch falsification and held-out RMSE answer different questions; neither stands in for the other.
And could held-out RMSE improve even if the placebo check is concerning?

Conceptually, yes. A predictor could achieve a favorable error comparison while a placebo-batch result calls its biological or transferable interpretation into question. The proposal should allow those outcomes to be reported separately rather than treating predictive improvement as a reason to disregard the falsification check.
How should I assess this proposal against the predictive goal?

Compare perturbation-response RMSE for the proposed use of unpaired ATAC with RNA-only models on the same holdout condition where both donors and perturbations are unseen. The stated target is a 15% relative reduction: the augmented prediction would need RMSE no greater than 0.85 times RNA-only RMSE. The proposal supplies a possible way to seek that improvement, not an RMSE value showing it has been achieved.
Would good performance on a donor-only holdout answer that question?

No. The requirement concerns unseen donors and perturbations together. Performance when only the donor is unseen, or only the perturbation is unseen, could be informative for a different question but would not by itself establish the 15% reduction under the joint condition.
Does the proposal identify biological RNA–ATAC coupling if it reaches the 15% reduction?

No. Reaching that reduction would establish a predictive comparison under the specified holdout. An identifiable biological coupling claim would additionally require assumptions and information that distinguish the relationship used for transport from batch-associated alternatives. The placebo check might challenge some alternatives, but neither predictive success nor a reassuring placebo result automatically supplies unique identification.
Where might separation remain impossible despite all three proposed components?

If the available donor–batch incidence does not distinguish donor from batch, or if batch-associated variation can mimic the relationship between module scores and RNA contrasts without producing a detectable placebo-batch signal, the biological explanation may remain ambiguous. Within-batch contrasts, weighting, and falsification cannot uniquely separate explanations that make the same observable predictions under the available information. That is a limit to characterize, not a claim that such a failure has already been observed here.
Should I present the proposal as replacing RNA-only prediction altogether?

No. It proposes using unpaired ATAC module scores to help transport RNA perturbation contrasts. RNA-only models remain the performance comparison for determining whether that additional information delivers the required improvement. Describing the approach as an alternative route to augmenting RNA-based prediction is more precise than implying RNA information or its baseline has been discarded.
What is a compact description that keeps the three components and their limits clear?

“Propose transporting within-batch RNA perturbation contrasts using unpaired ATAC module scores and donor-overlap weighting, with placebo-batch falsification to probe batch-driven interpretations. Evaluate prediction against RNA-only on joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdouts, while treating biological coupling as identifiable only where the available comparisons and assumptions distinguish it from batch effects.”
Do ATAC module scores predict perturbation-effect variation across donors, or do they merely encode batch structure after within-batch differencing?

That is the distinction to determine; the question does not yet supply an answer. A useful module score would carry information about how an RNA perturbation effect varies across donors beyond what batch structure explains. A batch proxy could instead appear associated with those effects because donors and batches are entangled. Within-batch differencing changes how the RNA effect is expressed, but it does not automatically establish which interpretation of the unpaired ATAC score is right.
Why doesn’t taking an RNA contrast within each batch settle the batch concern?

A within-batch contrast avoids interpreting a simple difference between batches as the RNA perturbation effect. But the ATAC module scores used to transport or predict variation in those contrasts may still track batch. Moreover, if the donors contributing contrasts differ across batches, apparent differences among donor effects can remain entangled with batch context. Differencing the RNA outcome does not, by itself, remove batch information from an unpaired ATAC predictor.
So even if the score is associated with the differenced RNA effect, that is not yet evidence of donor-specific biology?

Correct. An association is compatible with useful donor-related information, but also with a score that encodes how measurements or donor composition vary by batch. The question is whether the score distinguishes perturbation-effect variation among donors in a way that remains meaningful when the batch explanation is considered, rather than merely reexpressing that explanation.
What exactly is meant by perturbation-effect variation across donors?

It means that the RNA response contrast associated with a perturbation need not be the same for every donor. The proposed role of ATAC module scores is to help predict those differences across donors. That is distinct from predicting which batch a measurement belongs to or predicting an overall batch-associated shift.
Could a module score contain both donor-relevant information and batch information?

Yes. The alternatives in the question need not be mutually exclusive in every possible case. A score could reflect some transferable variation in perturbation effects while also encoding batch. The interpretation then depends on whether its contribution to predicting donor variation can be distinguished from, and persists beyond, the batch-associated component.
Does the fact that ATAC is unpaired make a score’s relationship to the RNA effect less direct?

Yes. The score and the RNA perturbation contrast are not supplied as a direct matched RNA–ATAC measurement for each unit. Relating them therefore requires a defensible correspondence or transport assumption. An observed predictive association cannot on its own demonstrate that a particular ATAC score measures the biological mechanism behind a particular RNA contrast.
What would be the conceptual difference between a batch proxy and a transferable predictor?

A batch proxy is informative largely because it tracks the observed batch arrangement. A transferable predictor remains informative about perturbation-effect variation when the relationship cannot rely on that particular arrangement, notably for the unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation setting of interest. Good prediction in an observed arrangement alone would not distinguish these possibilities.
If a score predicts which batch a sample came from, must it be useless for predicting perturbation effects?

No. Batch association does not prove the absence of donor-relevant information. It does, however, prevent treating an apparent score–effect relationship as unambiguously biological without further separation. The relevant question is whether the score contributes information about donor variation in perturbation effects that cannot be accounted for solely by batch structure.
Conversely, if it does not obviously predict batch, can I call it biological?

Not automatically. Failure to detect batch information by one characterization would not exclude all batch-related patterns, and it would not supply a direct biological correspondence between unpaired ATAC and RNA. It could lessen a specific concern, but the biological interpretation would still rest on the available comparisons and assumptions.
Where does donor overlap across batches matter to this question?

When donors appear across batch contexts, their overlap can help distinguish a donor-related pattern from one associated with a particular batch. It provides relevant contrasts for interpreting both the RNA effects and the ATAC scores. If donor and batch are inseparable in the available incidence pattern, a score associated with apparent donor differences may equally admit a batch-based interpretation unless additional constraints distinguish them.
Would donor-overlap weighting itself prove the scores reflect perturbation-effect variation?

No. Weighting can take the available donor overlap into account when transporting within-batch RNA contrasts, but it cannot create missing observations or validate the biological content of an ATAC module score. It is part of a proposed way to use the information, not a demonstration that the score is more than a batch proxy.
What role could a placebo-batch falsification check play in answering this?

It could challenge the claim that an apparent module-score relationship is specifically about transferable perturbation effects. If a batch-based placebo also produces an apparently persuasive relationship, that would raise concern about a batch proxy. A reassuring placebo result would address only the batch alternatives that the particular check can detect; it would not prove the score’s biological meaning.
Could within-batch contrasts still differ systematically between batches?

Conceptually, yes. Differencing within a batch removes a simple shared batch level from that contrast, but it does not guarantee that the contrasts, the donors represented, or the relationship to ATAC module scores are identical across batches. The question is precisely whether the apparent across-donor effect variation can be attributed to something transferable rather than to the remaining batch-linked structure.
If a score predicts donor differences within a batch, does that resolve the across-batch interpretation?

It would be relevant to the across-donor question within that batch, but would not alone establish transfer across batch contexts. A relationship found within a batch might not retain the same interpretation elsewhere, especially with unpaired modalities. Within-batch evidence and transfer across donor–batch contexts should not be treated as interchangeable.
What if the score improves prediction for unseen donors and perturbations?

That would address predictive transfer under the evaluated holdout conditions. For the broader goal, the specified benchmark is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations. Even a qualifying RMSE reduction would not, by itself, prove that the score reflects biological variation rather than every possible batch-related alternative; the interpretive question remains separate.
And if its holdout RMSE does not improve, can I conclude the score only encodes batch?

No. Lack of predictive improvement under a particular evaluation would not identify the score’s content uniquely. It might fail to help prediction without being purely batch-related. The narrow conclusion would concern predictive performance in that evaluation, not a proof that the score carries no donor-relevant biological information.
Is there an incidence pattern where this distinction simply cannot be made from the available information?

If the observed donor and batch structure provides no contrasts capable of separating them, and a batch-driven score and a donor-relevant score could explain the same association with the within-batch RNA contrasts, the explanations are observationally indistinguishable without additional assumptions. In that case one can still ask how well predictions perform, but should not claim the module score’s biological interpretation has been identified.
Does the question ask for a specific algorithm for constructing the module scores?

No. It asks what information the scores actually convey in relation to across-donor perturbation effects after within-batch differencing. The proposal mentions unpaired ATAC module scores, donor-overlap weighting, and placebo-batch falsification, but neither the score construction nor an algorithmic answer is specified here.
How should I express the question without presuming that either explanation is correct?

“After forming within-batch RNA perturbation contrasts, do unpaired ATAC module scores provide transferable information about variation in perturbation effects across donors, or can their apparent predictive value be explained by donor–batch structure?” That leaves both possibilities open and keeps predictive value distinct from proof of biological coupling.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: with crossed donors and batch-overlapping perturbations, residual ATAC module scores explain donor-specific RNA perturbation contrasts beyond batch labels and placebo modules. What exactly is being claimed?

It is a conditional claim about information in the ATAC scores, not a finding that the scores have already proved useful. Donors observed across batches and perturbations represented across batches provide two distinct kinds of overlap. Under those conditions, the hypothesis predicts that residual ATAC module scores account for variation in donor-specific RNA perturbation contrasts that batch labels and placebo modules do not account for. That would be more informative than an association attributable only to recorded batch structure or to the placebo comparison.
Why does the hypothesis require both crossed donors and batch-overlapping perturbations?

They address different potential ambiguities. Donor crossing supplies comparisons involving a donor across batch contexts. Perturbation overlap supplies comparisons involving a perturbation across batch contexts. One does not imply the other: an apparent difference among donors might track batch, while an apparent perturbation-specific pattern might also track batch if the pertinent perturbation never crosses it. The hypothesis is explicitly limited to conditions with both kinds of overlap.
Does batch-overlapping mean that every perturbation must appear in every batch?

No. It means perturbations are represented across batch contexts, rather than being exclusively associated with a single batch. The hypothesis does not specify a fully crossed layout, how many batches each perturbation spans, or a minimum count of overlapping perturbations. Any interpretation would need to consider whether the overlap supports the particular donor-specific contrasts being examined.
What are donor-specific RNA contrasts in this statement?

They are the RNA perturbation-response contrasts whose variation among donors is at issue. In the proposed approach, those contrasts are formed within batches before considering whether information from unpaired ATAC helps explain their donor-to-donor variation. A contrast for a donor is not, by itself, an ATAC measurement paired to that RNA observation.
What does “residual ATAC module scores” commit me to?

It says the claim concerns the residual component of the module scores, as opposed to simply treating their raw association with RNA contrasts as the proposed signal. But the hypothesis does not specify how residuals are calculated or which quantities are removed. It would be too specific to name a residualization algorithm or to assert that producing residual scores has already removed all batch structure.
Could a residual score still contain batch information?

Yes. Calling a score residual does not prove that every batch-related component has disappeared. The hypothesis asks whether whatever information remains explains the donor-specific contrasts beyond batch labels and placebo modules. If residual scores still encode relevant batch variation not captured by those comparisons, a biological interpretation would require further care.
Why compare with batch labels explicitly?

Batch labels represent an obvious competing explanation for an apparent relationship between ATAC scores and RNA contrasts. “Beyond batch labels” asks whether the residual scores account for donor-specific contrast variation that is not already accounted for by knowing batch assignment. It does not imply that batch labels capture every possible batch effect.
What do the placebo modules add to that comparison?

They provide an additional reference for asking whether the residual ATAC scores offer information distinctive to the proposed perturbation-effect relationship, rather than merely producing an apparent association of a kind also available from a placebo. The hypothesis does not define how the placebo modules are constructed, so their exact meaning and what alternatives they can test must not be assumed.
Does the word “beyond” mean the residual scores have to outperform each comparator separately?

The important interpretation is that their contribution should not be explained away by batch labels or by the placebo-module comparison. How that is quantified is not specified. It would be premature to assert a particular scoring rule, statistical test, or size of improvement. The hypothesis is about additional explanatory information relative to those references.
Could the scores appear informative simply because donors and batches are associated?

That is exactly the concern the hypothesis seeks to distinguish from donor-specific information. Crossed donors can supply relevant donor-across-batch comparisons, but their presence alone is no guarantee that every batch-associated pattern has been excluded. A score–contrast association must be considered against batch labels and placebo modules before being described as information beyond those references.
If the residual scores explain the contrasts beyond batch labels, does that establish biological coupling?

Not automatically. A contribution beyond recorded labels would make a simple explanation based solely on those labels less adequate under the comparison used. It would not exclude unmodeled batch-associated variation, validate the relationship between unpaired RNA and ATAC, or establish a causal biological mechanism. “Explain” here concerns the proposed relationship to variation in RNA contrasts, not proof of its unique biological origin.
Would surpassing placebo modules resolve that last concern?

It would address the alternatives represented by those placebo modules, provided they are suitable references. It would not eliminate every possible nuisance explanation merely because one placebo comparison is passed. The hypothesis requires an incremental contrast with both placebo modules and batch labels, but interpretation still depends on what those references can actually distinguish.
Could a score explain within-batch differences among donors yet fail to transfer to other donors?
