GateAudit v1 tabulates control-independence results, perturbation overlap, coupling-bound widths, three-donor joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE, and bound coverage. How should I describe what this artifact brings together?

Describe GateAudit v1 as a table that places the control diagnostic, perturbation–batch arrangement, coupling-bound properties, predictive error, and bound coverage side by side. That makes it possible to examine whether a gate’s predictive performance and the reliability of its bounds agree under the recorded conditions. The list of fields does not itself state any values, trends, or conclusions about which conditions qualify for ATAC use.
Why is the control-independence result a separate field from bound coverage?

They answer different questions. A control-independence result concerns whether the controls satisfy the specified diagnostic for perturbation association. Bound coverage concerns whether a coupling bound contains the quantity it is intended to cover. Passing the control diagnostic does not automatically establish coverage, and coverage does not by itself show that the controls passed the diagnostic.
Does the table say how the independence test was performed?

Not in the stated description. It says GateAudit v1 tabulates control-independence results, but does not give a test statistic, passing criterion, or procedure. A reader should not infer those details merely from the presence of the result field.
What does perturbation overlap tell me alongside the control result?

It keeps the perturbation–batch incidence condition visible when interpreting a control result or an RMSE value. A perturbation represented across batches offers a different comparison from one confined to a batch. The artifact description does not specify a numerical overlap measure or say how results differ across overlap conditions.
Is perturbation overlap the same thing as the three-donor condition?

No. Perturbation overlap concerns where perturbations occur across batches. The three-donor condition concerns donors; in this context, it refers to the three-cross-batch-donor setting for the joint-holdout RMSE. One kind of overlap does not establish the other.
Can I infer from the three-donor label which batches those donors connect?

No. A count of three cross-batch donors does not specify the complete donor–batch incidence pattern. GateAudit v1’s stated fields do not provide those connections, so a claim about which donor–batch contrasts are available would require more than the label alone.
What is the role of the coupling-bound-width field?

It reports how wide a coupling bound is for the entries being tabulated. That can help examine how restrictive a width-based gate is, but width alone says neither whether the bound covers its intended quantity nor whether it excludes a relevant batch-only explanation. It is also a different quantity from prediction RMSE.
Does a reported width tell me whether the bound excludes zero?

No. Width gives the span of the bound, not its position. Bounds of the same width can differ in whether they contain zero. The artifact description lists widths but does not say it tabulates bound endpoints or zero-exclusion decisions.
If a bound is narrow, may I assume it has good coverage?

No. A narrow bound may be informative if it reliably contains the intended coupling quantity, but it could also miss that quantity. The separate coverage field is important precisely because bound width cannot serve as a substitute for checking coverage.
What should I understand by the bound-coverage field?

It concerns whether the coupling bounds cover the coupling quantity they are intended to bound under the evaluated conditions. It is an assessment of the bounds, not a measurement of how close perturbation-response predictions are to their targets. The description does not provide a coverage rate or a threshold for judging one.
If coverage is reported as favorable, does that mean batch-only explanations have been excluded?

Not necessarily. A bound can contain the intended coupling quantity and still permit a batch-only explanation. Exclusion depends on what values and explanations the bound allows under the stated assumptions. Coverage and exclusion should therefore remain separate interpretive questions.
What is distinctive about the RMSE field?

It is joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE in the three-donor condition. It assesses predictive error when donor and perturbation are both unseen. It does not measure bound coverage, reveal how the controls behaved, or identify the biological origin of the predictive signal.
Could I read that RMSE as the RNA-only baseline?

Not from the field description. It says three-donor joint-holdout RMSE, without specifying an RNA-only RMSE field or identifying every predictor to which an entry belongs. A relative improvement versus RNA-only would require clearly labeled, comparable RMSE values on the same joint holdout.
So the presence of an RMSE column does not establish the 15% target?

Correct. The performance target requires perturbation-response RMSE at least 15% lower than RNA-only on comparable joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdouts. Knowing that GateAudit v1 tabulates joint-holdout RMSE does not supply the values or the corresponding RNA-only comparison needed to establish that reduction.
If an entry has low RMSE but poor bound coverage, how should those findings be kept apart?

A low RMSE would concern predictive performance for that entry. Poor coverage would raise a separate concern about relying on its bound to justify a coupling or gating interpretation. Neither observation cancels the other: predictive accuracy cannot repair an unreliable bound, and poor coverage does not change the RMSE that was measured. That is a possible way to read such an entry, not a finding stated by the artifact description.
Could coverage be good while the RMSE is disappointing?

Yes, conceptually. A bound can behave well as a bound without the resulting prediction improving enough on the joint holdout. GateAudit v1’s fields let those outcomes be discussed separately; its description does not say whether that combination occurs.
What if control-independence results differ across perturbation-overlap conditions?

That would be a condition-specific diagnostic pattern worth reporting with the overlap labels intact. It should not be reduced to a universal statement about all controls or all perturbations. The artifact description makes the comparison possible but does not report such a pattern.
Would a passing control-independence result certify biological RNA–ATAC coupling?

No. Passing a control diagnostic addresses the perturbation associations that diagnostic can detect. It does not, by itself, show that the coupling bound covers its target, that it excludes every relevant batch-only explanation, or that the unpaired RNA–ATAC relationship has a unique biological interpretation.
Does the artifact tell me how often a gate admits ATAC?

Not from its stated list of fields. It tabulates control-independence results, perturbation overlap, bound widths, three-donor joint-holdout RMSE, and bound coverage. Those fields do not necessarily reveal admission frequency or the complete admission rule, so neither should be inferred.
Can I use GateAudit v1 to claim that one perturbation-overlap arrangement is always better?

No. Its description does not provide RMSE or coverage results by arrangement, let alone establish a universal ordering. If entries are compared, conclusions should remain tied to the particular recorded overlap conditions and the outcome being compared.
What is a concise description that does not imply the gate has already been validated?

“GateAudit v1 tabulates control-independence results, perturbation overlap, coupling-bound widths, bound coverage, and three-donor joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE. It brings diagnostic, bounding, and predictive measurements together without their mere presence establishing valid batch separation or a 15% improvement versus RNA-only.”

Using GateAudit v1, I want to stratify the ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates with three cross-batch donors by control independence and perturbation overlap. Then I’ll test whether joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE is ≤0.68 and assess bound coverage. What does this activity separate?

It separates two conditions that could matter to the gates: whether the controls pass the perturbation-independence assessment, and whether the perturbations overlap across batches. Within each resulting stratum, joint-holdout RMSE addresses predictive performance, while bound coverage addresses the reliability of the coupling bounds. The activity specifies those comparisons but reports no stratum-specific results.
Why keep the three-cross-batch-donor condition fixed?

It keeps the stated donor-overlap count attached to every comparison in this activity. Differences between strata would then be described in terms of control independence and perturbation overlap within that three-donor setting. The count does not specify which batches the donors connect, and this activity does not test whether another donor-overlap count behaves the same way.
Does perturbation overlap refer to those same three donors?

No. The three cross-batch donors describe donor–batch incidence. Perturbation overlap describes whether a perturbation is represented across batch contexts. A condition can have donors crossing batches while its perturbations are batch-exclusive, so the two dimensions need separate labels.
Would the relevant perturbation strata be batch-exclusive and batch-bridging?

Those are the perturbation-overlap distinctions available for this discussion: batch-exclusive perturbations are confined to a batch context, while batch-bridging perturbations appear across batch contexts. Stratifying lets you inspect the RMSE and coverage within each arrangement rather than attributing a combined result to both.
And how should I describe the control-independence strata?

As conditions distinguished by the recorded control-independence result, such as passing versus failing the specified assessment. A passing result should not be renamed “uncontaminated” or “verified batch-only”; it reports what that assessment found, not every property of the controls.
Is this the same as comparing a screened gate with an unscreened gate?

Not as stated. This activity stratifies gates by control-independence results. Whether a control was screened is a procedural distinction; whether it passed or failed is a diagnostic result. GateAudit v1 tabulates the results, but this activity does not specify a screened-versus-unscreened comparison within each stratum.
Why not pool passing and failing controls if I only care about RMSE ≤0.68?

Pooling could hide whether the RMSE criterion is reached under both control-independence conditions or only one. It would also obscure whether bound coverage differs between them. The stratification preserves those distinctions without presuming that the results actually differ.
Should I compare control status within each perturbation-overlap condition?

Yes, that is one way to read the stratification: compare passing and failing controls while holding the perturbation-overlap category fixed. You can also compare perturbation-overlap categories while holding control status fixed. Keeping the comparisons distinct avoids attributing a difference to control independence when perturbation overlap has changed too.
What is being tested with the ≤0.68 RMSE value?

Whether the gated predictor’s perturbation-response RMSE on the joint donor–perturbation holdout is no greater than 0.68 in each evaluated stratum. It is a predictive threshold, not a coupling-bound width or a coverage threshold. The activity does not say which strata, if any, satisfy it.
How does that threshold relate to the 15% improvement requirement?

If the comparable RNA-only RMSE on the same joint holdout is 0.80, then 0.68 is exactly 15% lower: (0.80 − 0.68) / 0.80 = 15%. Testing RMSE ≤0.68 is therefore relevant to that benchmark under that baseline. The activity itself does not report an RNA-only RMSE for each stratum, so the relative comparison should not be assumed to hold across differing baselines.
Does “joint” require both dimensions to be unseen?

Yes. The prediction evaluation concerns both a held-out donor and a held-out perturbation. A donor-only RNA-contrast RMSE or a perturbation-only holdout would not be the joint-holdout RMSE named in this activity.
Could a stratum reach RMSE ≤0.68 but have poor bound coverage?

Conceptually, yes. The predictor could meet the numerical error threshold while its coupling bounds fail to contain the quantity they are intended to cover. That would preserve a predictive finding but weaken reliance on the bounds as a justification for interpreting the gate. The activity measures both precisely so that neither outcome is inferred from the other.
And could a stratum have good coverage but miss the RMSE threshold?
Yes. Coverage concerns whether the bounds behave as intended; it does not guarantee that the resulting predictions are accurate enough to reach ≤0.68. The activity leaves both outcomes open.
What does bound coverage refer to without a stated cutoff?

It refers to whether the coupling bounds contain their intended coupling quantity under the evaluated conditions. GateAudit v1 includes a coverage field, but neither this activity nor the artifact description supplies a numerical coverage target. It would be inaccurate to declare coverage adequate using an unstated threshold.
Does a bound covering its target prove that a batch-only explanation has been ruled out?

No. A bound can cover the intended coupling quantity while still including values compatible with a batch-only explanation. Coverage checks reliability in one sense; whether the bound excludes the relevant batch-only alternatives requires examining what it contains and the assumptions connecting those alternatives to coupling.
Do the ≤0.20 gates necessarily exclude zero?

The activity specifies the ≤0.20 width criterion but does not explicitly state the zero-exclusion result for every bound in the strata. Width alone cannot tell you whether a bound contains zero. Even a zero-excluding bound would need a defensible interpretation before treating it as excluding every relevant batch-only explanation.
Could a wide-looking bound and a low RMSE be compared directly?

They can be reported for the same stratum, but they are different measurements. Bound width is on the coupling scale; RMSE is prediction error. There is no direct conversion from a width at or below 0.20 into a joint-holdout RMSE at or below 0.68.
If a passing-control, batch-exclusive stratum meets the RMSE threshold, can I say perturbation bridging is unnecessary?

You could say that the numerical RMSE threshold was met in that evaluated batch-exclusive stratum, if that is what the measurements show. It would not establish a general rule that bridging is unnecessary for identifying target coupling or for prediction in every control and donor-overlap setting. No such stratum result is provided by this activity.
What if a failing-control, batch-bridging stratum also meets it?

That would be another condition-specific predictive result. It would not turn the failing controls into passing ones or establish that their associated bounds have good coverage. The purpose of retaining both stratification labels is to report such a result without erasing the control diagnostic.
Would either of those possible RMSE results prove biological RNA–ATAC coupling?

No. Meeting an RMSE threshold assesses prediction, while identifying biological coupling requires distinguishing it from permitted batch-only explanations under valid bounds and assumptions. The control-independence result and bound coverage are relevant, but neither can be replaced by prediction accuracy.
Can this activity establish that three cross-batch donors are the minimum needed?

No. Every comparison here is specified for the three-cross-batch-donor condition. Without evaluating other donor-overlap counts in this activity, a result cannot identify a minimum or establish sufficiency for all arrangements of three donors.
Does this activity say anything about how much contamination is present in each stratum?

It calls for stratification by control independence and perturbation overlap, and for testing RMSE and coverage in the stated three-donor, ≤0.20-gate setting. It does not specify a contamination percentage for each stratum. Control-test status should not be converted into an unreported contamination level.
How should I read the results if RMSE and coverage give different impressions across strata?

Keep each outcome attached to its control-independence and perturbation-overlap labels. A stratum’s RMSE answers whether its predictions meet the specified numerical threshold; its coverage answers whether its coupling bounds contain their intended quantity. Differences between those outcomes are informative precisely because a predictive success need not validate a bound, and a reliable bound need not ensure the required predictive accuracy.
What is a concise statement of the activity without implying it has already found a qualifying stratum?

“Using GateAudit v1, stratify ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates with three cross-batch donors by control-independence result and perturbation overlap, then assess bound coverage and test whether joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdout RMSE is ≤0.68 in each evaluated stratum.”

GateAudit v1 reports that batch-exclusive gates with three crossed donors and independence-passing controls yielded joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE of 0.67, versus 0.80 for RNA-only. What is the direct finding?

In that reported condition, the gated predictor had lower joint-holdout RMSE than the RNA-only comparator: 0.67 versus 0.80. The result is specific to batch-exclusive perturbations, three donors crossing batches, and controls that passed the perturbation-independence assessment. It is a predictive comparison, not a finding about why the predictions improved.
What is the absolute difference between those errors?
The difference is 0.80 − 0.67 = 0.13 RMSE. That is an absolute difference on the reported RMSE scale; no units for that scale are specified.
Can I express it as a relative reduction?

Yes. Using RNA-only RMSE as the denominator, 0.13 / 0.80 = 0.1625, so the gated RMSE is 16.25% lower than RNA-only in this reported comparison. That percentage summarizes the joint holdout, not the improvement for every individual prediction.
Why use 0.80 rather than 0.67 as the denominator?
Because the relative comparison is against RNA-only. The RNA-only RMSE of 0.80 is the baseline from which the reduction is calculated. Dividing by 0.67 would answer a different percentage question.
Does “batch-exclusive” mean the donors were each confined to a batch?

No. Batch-exclusive describes the perturbations: they do not bridge batches in this condition. The donors are described separately as crossed, with three donors appearing across batch contexts. Perturbation–batch incidence and donor–batch incidence should not be conflated.
Does the count of three crossed donors specify the full incidence pattern?

No. It identifies how many donors crossed batches, but not which batches they connected or how their observations were distributed. The RMSE comparison should be attributed to the reported three-crossed-donor condition without assuming that every arrangement with that count behaves the same way.
What does it mean that the controls were independence-passing?

It means the controls passed the specified perturbation-independence assessment. That is the diagnostic status attached to this result. It does not, by itself, prove that the control peaks contain only batch-associated variation or that they represent every relevant batch effect.
Can I call them uncontaminated controls, then?

No. Test passage and absence of contamination are different claims. This finding specifies that the controls passed an independence assessment; it does not state their contamination level or establish that they are wholly free of biological signal.
Do we know whether the passing controls caused the lower RMSE?

Not from these two RMSE values. They compare a gated predictor in the stated passing-control condition with RNA-only. They do not isolate the effect of control status through an otherwise matched passing-versus-failing comparison. The controls’ test result is part of the condition, not a measured causal explanation for the difference.
Could I say this is a screened-versus-unscreened result?

No. The reported comparison is gated RMSE versus RNA-only RMSE. Although control-independence status is specified, the finding does not identify a screened and an unscreened RMSE arm or quantify the effect of conducting a screen.
What exactly does the joint holdout tell me?

The predictive error is assessed with donor and perturbation both unseen in the holdout setting. It should not be relabeled as an error for held-out donors alone or for perturbations alone. The two RMSE values are comparable in the stated joint evaluation.
Is the 0.67 error stated for every held-out donor and perturbation?
No. RMSE summarizes errors over the reported holdout. It does not give errors for individual donor–perturbation predictions or show that the gated predictor improved every one of them.
Does the evidence show how often the gate admitted ATAC?
No. The reported RMSE is for the gated approach, but no admission frequency or case-by-case gate decision is supplied. An aggregate predictive error cannot tell us how many predictions used ATAC.
Does it give the actual widths or endpoints of the coupling bounds?

No. Even if a gate is evaluated under a bound-width criterion, the 0.67 and 0.80 figures are RMSE values, not bound widths. This finding provides no individual bound endpoints or widths and does not show whether a particular bound included zero.
What about bound coverage? Is that implied by the favorable RMSE?

No. Bound coverage asks whether the coupling bounds contain the quantity they are meant to cover. This finding supplies no coverage measurement. Lower prediction error does not demonstrate that the bounds were reliable or that their interpretation excluded a batch-only explanation.
Does the control test, together with the RMSE comparison, identify biological RNA–ATAC coupling?

Not on its own. Passing the control diagnostic addresses the perturbation association that test can detect; the RMSE comparison addresses prediction. Neither establishes that the coupling bounds cover their target or that all relevant batch-only accounts have been distinguished from biological coupling. The finding should remain a condition-specific predictive result.
Can I infer what the gated predictor would do with batch-bridging perturbations?

No. The reported stratum is batch-exclusive. Its 0.67 RMSE should not be assigned to batch-bridging perturbations, and the comparison does not establish a ranking between exclusive and bridging arrangements.
Can I infer the behavior of controls that fail the independence assessment?
No failing-control RMSE is reported in this GateAudit v1 finding. It does not establish the prediction error or bound behavior for that other control-status condition.
Does this establish a minimum of three crossed donors?

No. The result is observed with three crossed donors. It does not report comparable conditions with different donor-overlap counts, so it cannot establish a minimum or show that the count alone determines predictive performance.
What if I want to avoid assigning the predictive difference to any one ingredient?

Keep all the conditions together when reporting the observation and state only the measured comparison. The RMSE difference cannot be partitioned among donor crossing, control-test status, gating, or the batch-exclusive perturbation arrangement from this finding alone.
Give me a short reporting sentence.

“In GateAudit v1, batch-exclusive gates with three crossed donors and perturbation-independence-passing controls had joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE of 0.67 versus 0.80 for RNA-only, a 16.25% relative reduction. Bound coverage and biological identifiability are not established by this comparison.”

I’ve decided to deploy ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates with three crossed donors. For batch-exclusive perturbations, the controls must pass the perturbation-independence test; for batch-bridging perturbations, the gates may be used even if the controls fail it. Can you help me state the rule precisely?

“Deploy ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates in the three-crossed-donor setting. Require perturbation-independence-passing controls for batch-exclusive perturbations; permit batch-bridging perturbations even when controls fail that test.” This is a conditional deployment rule. It does not say that a failed control test is desirable, or that passing the rule proves biological RNA–ATAC coupling.
Does ≤0.20 describe the allowed control contamination?
No. It is the ceiling on coupling-bound width for the gates. Control-test status is a separate condition, and this decision does not set a numerical contamination limit.
If a coupling bound is wider than 0.20, does the decision permit deploying that gate in a batch-bridging condition?

No. The ≤0.20 width criterion applies to the deployed gates regardless of perturbation overlap or control-test status. The exception for batch-bridging perturbations concerns failing controls; it does not waive the gate-width condition.
And what does “three crossed donors” specify?

It specifies the donor–batch setting for deployment: three donors cross batch contexts. It is not a count of perturbations or a statement that there are three batches. The decision does not describe which batches those donors connect or establish a rule for a different donor-overlap setting.
Are batch-exclusive perturbations disallowed whenever the controls fail the independence test?

Yes, under this deployment decision. The batch-exclusive branch requires controls that pass the perturbation-independence test. If they fail, that branch does not satisfy the rule, even if the gate’s coupling-bound width is ≤0.20 and three donors cross batches.
What if the controls have not been tested?

Untested controls have not been shown to pass, so they do not meet the stated requirement for batch-exclusive perturbations. That is different from claiming they would fail if tested. The decision provides no separate rule that treats unknown status as passing.
Does passing the test mean the controls contain no biological signal?

No. It means they satisfy the specified perturbation-independence assessment. Passing that assessment should not be expanded into a claim that the controls are biologically inert, represent every relevant batch effect, or validate the coupling bounds in all respects.
What exactly is relaxed for batch-bridging perturbations?

Only the requirement that controls pass the independence test. Batch-bridging perturbations may be included even if the controls fail. The ≤0.20 gate-width ceiling and three-crossed-donor deployment setting still apply. “Allow despite failing controls” does not mean the controls are reclassified as independent.
Does the bridging branch require the controls to fail?

No. It permits deployment despite failure; it does not require failure. A batch-bridging condition with passing controls is not excluded by that wording. The important distinction is that failing controls bar the batch-exclusive branch but do not, by themselves, bar the batch-bridging branch.
Why not call the batch-bridging exception a waiver of all control concerns?

Because a failed independence test remains a diagnostic warning. The decision permits use of the specified gate with batch-bridging perturbations despite that warning; it does not make the controls suitable as an unquestioned batch-only reference or establish that all batch-driven explanations have been eliminated.
Do crossed donors and batch-bridging perturbations mean the same thing?

No. Crossed donors are donors represented across batch contexts. Batch-bridging perturbations are perturbations represented across batch contexts. The decision sets a common three-crossed-donor condition and then applies different control-test requirements according to perturbation overlap. One kind of crossing does not imply the other.
If a perturbation is batch-exclusive, can donor crossing alone satisfy the control requirement?

No. Three crossed donors are required for deployment, but batch-exclusive perturbations also require independence-passing controls. The donor-overlap condition and the control condition are cumulative in that branch, not substitutes for one another.
Should I describe the rule as guaranteeing that the coupling is identifiable whenever deployment is allowed?

No. It decides when to deploy the ≤0.20 gates under the specified conditions. A deployment decision is not, by itself, a proof that a coupling bound covers its intended quantity or that the relevant biological and batch-only accounts are uniquely separated. Those interpretive claims would require their own justification.
Does permission to deploy in a batch-bridging condition mean the failed controls can be ignored when interpreting the result?

No. The prediction may be made under the decision, but the failed independence test should remain visible in any interpretation of the controls and coupling bounds. Permission to use a gate and confidence in a particular biological explanation are distinct.
Is this a rule about all RNA–ATAC predictors?

No. Its scope is the deployment of these ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates with three crossed donors. It distinguishes batch-exclusive from batch-bridging perturbations by the control-independence requirement. It does not prescribe conditions for every possible predictor using unpaired ATAC.
Does the rule itself say that deploying the gates reduces joint-holdout RMSE by at least 15% versus RNA-only?

No. This decision states where the gates may be deployed and when passing controls are required. It does not give an RMSE value or a performance guarantee for every permitted prediction. The ≥15% comparison with RNA-only on unseen donors and perturbations is a separate predictive claim.
Could a permitted batch-bridging case still have a questionable biological interpretation?

Yes. In particular, if its controls fail perturbation-independence testing, that failure remains relevant even though the decision allows deployment. Meeting the gate-width and donor-overlap conditions does not automatically establish that an ATAC contribution is biological rather than batch-related.
How should I write the decision so a reader cannot mistake “allow” for “require”?

You could say: “With three crossed donors, deploy ≤0.20 coupling-bound gates for batch-exclusive perturbations only if controls pass perturbation-independence testing. For batch-bridging perturbations, allow deployment even if controls fail that testing.” The second sentence grants an exception; it does not require failing controls.
Is it fair to say that the passing-control requirement depends on perturbation overlap?

Yes. That is the central distinction in the rule. Batch-exclusive perturbations need independence-passing controls, whereas batch-bridging perturbations may proceed despite independence-failing controls, under the same stated bound-width and three-crossed-donor conditions.
And if I give a brief qualification after the rule?

Add that deployment under the rule is not a certification of bound coverage, biological coupling, or a guaranteed RMSE improvement. In particular, a failing control test remains a limitation to disclose for any permitted batch-bridging condition.

Using GateAudit v1, I’m testing gated RNA–ATAC against RNA-only on PerturbTransfer-6 unseen-donor/perturbation holdouts. I also want to assess whether RMSE improves by at least 15% and examine identifiability in nested donor–batch designs. How should I frame this activity?

Frame it as two assessments on the stated holdouts. The predictive assessment compares perturbation-response RMSE for gated RNA–ATAC and RNA-only when both donor and perturbation are unseen, asking whether the relative reduction reaches ≥15%. The identifiability assessment asks what, if anything, a nested donor–batch design can distinguish about biological RNA–ATAC coupling versus batch effects. GateAudit v1 supplies relevant gate, control, overlap, and bound information, but this activity does not report either assessment’s outcome.
What does the name PerturbTransfer-6 tell us about the holdouts?

It identifies the holdouts used for this test. The activity says they involve unseen donors and perturbations; it does not specify the number of donors, the number of batches, how the holdouts are assigned, or what the “6” denotes. Those details should not be inferred from the name.
Should I call them joint holdouts?

Yes, so long as you retain the stated condition that both donor and perturbation are unseen for the prediction being evaluated. That is different from evaluating an unseen donor with a perturbation already available during fitting, or an unseen perturbation in an already-seen donor.
How exactly do I check the ≥15% RMSE requirement?

Compare gated RNA–ATAC and RNA-only perturbation-response RMSE on comparable PerturbTransfer-6 unseen-donor/perturbation holdouts. The gated RMSE must be no greater than 0.85 times the RNA-only RMSE. The activity supplies no RMSE values, so it does not yet say whether the requirement is met.
Could I establish that improvement from a low gated RMSE alone?
No. “At least 15% improvement” is a relative claim against RNA-only. Without a corresponding RNA-only RMSE on the same holdout condition, a gated RMSE alone cannot establish the percentage reduction.
What makes this an evaluation of gated RNA–ATAC, rather than simply an evaluation of ATAC?

The predictor being tested is the gated RNA–ATAC approach: ATAC contributes conditionally under the gate rather than being assumed usable in every case. The RMSE comparison evaluates the predictions produced by that approach as a whole. It does not, without further information, say how often ATAC was admitted or isolate the contribution of any single part of the gate.
Does using GateAudit v1 tell us which predictions received ATAC?

GateAudit v1 tabulates control-independence results, perturbation overlap, coupling-bound widths, three-donor joint-holdout RMSE, and bound coverage. Those fields provide context for examining a gate, but the artifact description alone does not specify case-by-case ATAC admission on PerturbTransfer-6. Do not infer an admission count from the name of the artifact or from an aggregate RMSE.
Is the three-donor RMSE recorded in GateAudit v1 automatically the RMSE for this test?

No. This activity specifically calls for testing gated RNA–ATAC against RNA-only on PerturbTransfer-6 holdouts. A recorded three-donor joint-holdout RMSE should not be relabeled as a PerturbTransfer-6 result without information connecting the evaluations. The new test needs its own clearly labeled comparison.
How should bound coverage enter the interpretation?

Coverage bears on whether the coupling bounds contain the coupling quantity they are intended to cover. That matters to the justification for gating ATAC, but it is not the same as prediction error. A favorable RMSE comparison would not establish bound coverage, and coverage would not guarantee the ≥15% RMSE reduction.
Does a narrow bound alone exclude batch-only explanations?

No. Width describes how broad a bound is, not which explanations it permits. To justify an interpretive claim, the bound must be valid under its assumptions and actually exclude the relevant batch-only accounts. A narrow bound that still permits such an account—or one whose construction is unreliable—cannot establish biological coupling simply through its width.
What should the nested-design identifiability assessment ask specifically?

It should ask whether, under the stated model and available information, donor-associated and batch-associated variation can be distinguished well enough to attribute an apparent RNA–ATAC relationship to biology. When donors are completely nested within batches and separate donor and batch effects are unrestricted, the incidence pattern alone cannot separate them: a batch-associated difference can be reassigned among the donors confined to that batch without changing the observations. Any stronger conclusion in a nested design would have to identify additional restrictions or information on which it relies.
If a nested design has good PerturbTransfer-6 RMSE, would that settle its identifiability?

No. Good prediction on jointly unseen donors and perturbations would be a performance result. It would not create the donor-across-batch contrasts missing from a completely nested design or establish that biological coupling has been uniquely separated from batch effects. The predictive and identifiability findings should remain separately stated.
Would poor RMSE prove that the nested design is nonidentifiable?

No. Poor predictive performance and structural nonidentifiability are different conclusions. An identifiability assessment concerns whether distinct biological and batch explanations can yield the same observations under the allowed assumptions. RMSE measures how accurately the approach predicts held-out perturbation responses.
Does a nested layout make every possible coupling quantity impossible to identify?

That would be too broad without specifying the coupling quantity and permissible assumptions. Complete nesting prevents separation of unrestricted donor and batch contributions from donor–batch incidence alone. Other constraints might narrow a particular target-specific relationship, but any such claim would rely on those constraints rather than on donor crossing supplied by the nested layout.
What role could GateAudit v1’s control-independence and perturbation-overlap fields play here?

They let you keep two relevant qualifiers visible: whether controls pass their stated diagnostic and whether perturbations bridge batches. Neither field automatically resolves donor–batch nesting. They can inform how a gated result is interpreted, but they do not replace a direct assessment of which biological and batch-only explanations remain compatible with the design and bounds.
Should I expect PerturbTransfer-6 to contain both crossed and nested layouts?

The activity says to assess nested-design identifiability, but it does not describe the incidence patterns represented within PerturbTransfer-6 or specify how that assessment is implemented. It would be premature to claim that the named holdouts contain a particular number or arrangement of crossed and nested cases.
Can the ≥15% prediction criterion and the nested-design question reach different conclusions?

Yes. One concerns relative perturbation-response RMSE on the specified unseen-donor/perturbation holdouts; the other concerns whether the available design and assumptions distinguish coupling from batch effects in nested layouts. The activity deliberately assesses both without treating either as a substitute for the other. It does not state the outcome of either assessment.
What is a concise description of the activity without implying results?

“Using GateAudit v1, compare gated RNA–ATAC with RNA-only on PerturbTransfer-6 holdouts where donors and perturbations are unseen, testing for a ≥15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE. Separately assess identifiability in nested donor–batch designs, including whether biological coupling can be distinguished from batch effects under the stated assumptions.”

PerturbTransfer-6 reports gated joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE of 0.67 versus 0.80 for RNA-only, or 16.3% lower, with three crossed donors. Nested designs defaulted to RNA-only. What is the direct result?

In the reported three-crossed-donor condition, gated RNA–ATAC had lower perturbation-response RMSE than RNA-only on holdouts where both donor and perturbation were unseen: 0.67 versus 0.80. Separately, the gated approach defaulted to RNA-only in nested designs. The finding does not give a nested-design RMSE or explain which gate condition led to that default.
Can you check how 16.3% was calculated?
The absolute difference is 0.80 − 0.67 = 0.13. Dividing by the RNA-only RMSE of 0.80 gives 0.1625, or 16.25%. Reported to one decimal place, that is 16.3% lower.
Why is 0.80 the denominator?
Because the relative reduction is stated versus RNA-only. Its RMSE of 0.80 is the comparison baseline. The gated RMSE of 0.67 is the value being compared with it.
What does the joint holdout tell me about the scope of the prediction result?

It means the reported predictive comparison concerns unseen donors and unseen perturbations together. The 0.67 versus 0.80 comparison should not be relabeled as a donor-only or perturbation-only result. Nor does an aggregate RMSE establish that every individual held-out prediction improved.
Does “three crossed donors” mean three batches?
No. It means three donors crossed batch contexts. The finding does not state how many batches each donor appeared in or which batches they connected.
Can I infer that three crossed donors are the minimum needed for this RMSE?

No. The result identifies the donor-overlap condition accompanying the reported RMSE. It gives no otherwise comparable PerturbTransfer-6 RMSE values for other numbers of crossed donors, so it does not establish a minimum.
Does donor crossing tell us whether the held-out perturbations bridged batches?

No. Donor–batch crossing and perturbation–batch bridging are different properties. This finding specifies three crossed donors and a joint donor–perturbation holdout, but does not state the perturbation–batch incidence pattern.
How should I interpret the nested designs defaulting to RNA-only?

It describes the predictor’s behavior in those designs: it used the RNA-only default rather than an ATAC-assisted prediction. It does not give the nested designs’ predictive error or, by itself, demonstrate why the gate took that path.
So I should not assign the 0.80 RMSE to the nested designs?

Correct. The 0.80 value is the RNA-only comparator for the reported three-crossed-donor joint-holdout result. Saying nested designs defaulted to RNA-only does not supply their RMSE, and it would be unwarranted to assign them that same number.
Does the nested default establish that coupling was nonidentifiable there?

Not from this finding alone. Defaulting to RNA-only tells us what the gated predictor did, not which identifiability assessment or bound condition determined that behavior. An assertion about impossibility of separating biological coupling from batch effects would require the relevant design and assumptions to be stated.
Does the lower RMSE with three crossed donors establish biological RNA–ATAC coupling?

No. It establishes a predictive comparison in that reported condition. The RMSE values do not show whether the coupling bounds had adequate coverage or whether the ATAC contribution could be distinguished from every relevant batch-only explanation. Predictive accuracy and biological identifiability remain separate claims.
Can I say the gate admitted ATAC for all predictions in the crossed-donor condition?

No. The result reports RMSE for the gated approach, not its case-by-case admission decisions. A gated predictor can produce an aggregate RMSE without ATAC being used for every prediction. The finding does not report how often ATAC contributed.
Do we know whether the controls passed an independence test in PerturbTransfer-6?

The fallback is a caution about what can be supported, not a declaration that ATAC is biologically empty.
Would additive batch effects alone guarantee that the coupling bounds have good coverage?

No. The decision defines where gated ATAC is retained, but does not replace checking whether the bounds behave as intended or whether other assumptions behind them hold. An additive-batch description is part of the intended scope, not an automatic certification of the bound construction.
Can I call every retained additive-batch result biologically identifiable?

That would be too strong. Retaining gated ATAC means it may contribute under the proposed gate in the stated design class. Identifying biological RNA–ATAC coupling still requires the bounds and available contrasts to exclude the relevant batch-only explanations under defensible assumptions. The decision does not declare that all such results have a unique biological interpretation.
How does donor overlap fit into this decision?

Donor overlap remains relevant to whether the bounds can distinguish donor-associated from batch-associated variation. This decision specifies additive-batch designs for retaining gated ATAC and coverage threats from donor-by-batch interactions for falling back. It does not state a new donor-overlap count or say that additivity can replace missing donor-across-batch comparisons.
Does this decision also specify whether perturbations must bridge batches?

No perturbation-overlap condition is stated in this decision. Its boundary is additive batch effects versus donor-by-batch interactions that threaten bound coverage. Do not add a requirement that all perturbations bridge batches, or infer that they never need to, from this sentence alone.
If controls appear reassuring, can I ignore donor-by-batch interactions?

No. A control result might constrain some batch-associated patterns, but it does not automatically establish coverage of coupling bounds when batch effects differ by donor. The fallback condition explicitly calls attention to interactions that threaten coverage; reassuring controls alone should not be treated as overriding that threat.
Is there a specified percentage of donor-by-batch interaction that triggers fallback?
No. This decision gives no numeric interaction-strength threshold. It hinges on whether interactions threaten coupling-bound coverage, not on a percentage supplied as a universal rule.
Does RNA-only fallback mean the model must be retrained in a particular way?

The decision does not specify an implementation. It says to rely on RNA-only prediction rather than the gated ATAC contribution when the coverage threat applies. A particular training procedure, ensemble weight, or switching algorithm would be an additional detail not stated here.
How should I discuss predictive performance under this rule?

Keep it separate from the decision to admit ATAC. When gated ATAC is retained, its perturbation-response RMSE can be compared with RNA-only under the same holdout conditions, especially unseen donors and perturbations. When fallback is triggered, describe that choice as a response to bound-coverage concerns rather than asserting an unreported RMSE advantage for RNA-only.
Does the rule itself meet the 15% improvement requirement?

No. A use rule does not supply an RMSE result for every condition it covers. The performance requirement remains a reduction of at least 15% versus RNA-only on jointly unseen donors and perturbations; the decision says when a gated ATAC contribution should be retained or withheld based on the batch-effect assumptions and bound coverage.
Could a nested donor–batch design qualify simply because its batch effects are additive?

Additivity alone does not create the donor-across-batch contrasts absent under complete nesting. This decision should not be read as overriding a separate identifiability problem caused by a nested incidence pattern. Retaining gated ATAC requires the relevant gate and separation assumptions to be supportable, not merely a label of additive batch effects.
What is the narrowest faithful statement of the decision?

“Retain gated ATAC in additive-batch designs, and fall back to RNA-only when donor-by-batch interactions threaten coupling-bound coverage.” If further explanation is needed, add that the fallback reflects uncertainty in the bounds, not proof that ATAC lacks biological information or that RNA-only is more accurate in every interaction setting.

I’m implementing TransferGate v1 with rank and donor-overlap checks, control-independence checks, perturbation-bridging checks, transport-eligibility checks, and donor-by-batch interaction checks. I also want to benchmark joint-holdout RMSE and fallbacks for nonidentifiable designs. How should I frame this activity?

Frame TransferGate v1 as an implementation being evaluated, not as a completed demonstration of transfer or identifiability. Its checks address different reasons that unpaired ATAC information might or might not be justified for perturbation-response prediction. The benchmark asks whether the resulting predictions improve on RNA-only models when both donors and perturbations are unseen. The fallback assessment asks whether designs that do not support the intended coupling interpretation are handled without treating uncertain ATAC information as identified biological signal.
Why put rank and overlap in the same list of checks?

They probe different prerequisites. Rank concerns whether the information used to relate RNA and ATAC has enough independent distinctions for the coupling claim at issue. Donor overlap concerns whether observations connect donors across batches in a way that can distinguish donor-associated variation from batch-associated variation. One cannot automatically substitute for the other: informative cross-modality structure does not create missing donor–batch comparisons, and donor overlap does not make redundant anchors informative.
Does a rank check mean counting anchors?

Not necessarily. Rank concerns independent information, whereas a count can include anchors that repeat one another. The activity does not specify a rank threshold or even a single anchor representation for every use of ATAC, so the implementation description should name the rank check without assigning it an unstated numerical rule.
What should the donor-overlap check look for conceptually?

It should assess whether the donor–batch incidence pattern supports the distinctions on which a proposed coupling claim relies. The number of donors appearing across batches is relevant, but their connections also matter: a count alone need not show which batches can be compared. Calling a design crossed should not be treated as a complete identifiability argument.
How does control independence differ from donor overlap?

Control independence concerns whether peaks used as controls show perturbation-associated behavior that compromises their intended reference role. Donor overlap concerns which donor–batch contrasts exist. A favorable control diagnostic cannot create a missing donor-across-batch observation; donor crossing cannot establish that a control peak is independent of perturbation.
If controls pass an independence check, may TransferGate v1 call them biologically inert?

No. Passing a specified diagnostic addresses the associations that diagnostic can detect. It does not prove an absence of all biological signal or guarantee that the controls capture every relevant batch effect. TransferGate v1 can retain the diagnostic result as a condition for interpreting a gate decision without elevating it to a universal certificate.
Why does the implementation also need a perturbation-bridging check?

A donor can appear across batches while a perturbation remains confined to one batch. The bridging check keeps that distinction visible by asking whether the pertinent perturbation is represented across batch contexts. A perturbation bridge can provide a contrast relevant to separating its response from batch, but neither a bridge nor a donor crossing alone settles every possible batch-driven explanation.
Does bridging imply that the perturbation must occur in every batch?

No. Bridging means representation across batch contexts; it does not, as stated here, require a perturbation in every batch. The implementation activity does not specify a minimum number of connections or a universal rule for which bridging patterns suffice.
What is transport eligibility checking that the other checks are not?

It concerns whether the proposed use of unpaired ATAC information to carry an RNA perturbation contrast into a new prediction setting is warranted for the case being evaluated. Rank, donor overlap, controls, and perturbation bridging provide relevant information, but transport eligibility is a question about using the resulting relationship for prediction beyond the context in which the RNA contrast was observed. This activity does not specify the exact eligibility rule.
So I should not say a case is transport-eligible merely because an ATAC module score exists?

Correct. A module score is an input, not evidence that its relationship to an RNA contrast transfers to unseen donors and perturbations. Because RNA and ATAC are unpaired, the cross-modality relationship also rests on assumptions or constraints that should not be hidden by the existence of a score.
What do the interaction checks add to the implementation?

They address the possibility that batch-associated ATAC variation differs by donor. Under that possibility, a donor-across-batch contrast need not reflect a common additive batch effect, and a coupling bound constructed for a simpler account could be misleading. An interaction check makes that threat explicit instead of treating overlap and a narrow bound as automatic permission to use ATAC.
Would a detected donor-by-batch interaction always prove biological coupling cannot be identified?

No. Whether coupling can be separated depends on which interactions are allowed, what observations constrain them, and the particular coupling quantity at issue. The check is relevant to the reliability of an identification claim; the activity does not supply a universal interaction cutoff or declare every interaction fatal.
Should the checks be described as one combined pass–fail test?

That would lose useful distinctions. A design might have informative rank but insufficient donor overlap, or relevant perturbation bridging but controls that do not pass their diagnostic. Describing the checks separately keeps the reason for any withheld ATAC contribution or qualified interpretation visible. The activity does not specify a single aggregate score or an ordering of the checks.
Does implementing the checks mean their thresholds and order have already been fixed?

No. The stated activity names the checks and the benchmark, but gives no complete decision sequence, numeric thresholds for each check, or implementation formula. It is accurate to say TransferGate v1 is being implemented with those checks; it would add unsupported details to describe exactly how it resolves every combination of check outcomes.
What does a fallback for a nonidentifiable design accomplish?

It provides a prediction path that does not rely on treating an unresolved RNA–ATAC relationship as identifiable. For example, an RNA-only path can avoid admitting an ATAC contribution when the available design and assumptions cannot distinguish it from batch effects. A fallback does not prove that ATAC contains no biological information, and the activity does not report how often a fallback is used.
Could a completely nested donor–batch layout be relevant to that assessment?

Yes, as a general case to examine. When each donor appears in only one batch, the incidence pattern supplies no same-donor comparison across batches. If donor and batch contributions are both unrestricted, they cannot be separated from that pattern alone. A fallback assessment can ask whether the intended gate refrains from making a stronger coupling claim in such a case, while remaining clear about any additional assumptions that might constrain a narrower quantity.
If the fallback produces accurate predictions, does that resolve the identifiability issue?

No. Predicting well and separating biological coupling from batch effects are different outcomes. A fallback can be useful precisely because a prediction is still possible without asserting that an ambiguous ATAC relationship has been identified. Its predictive error should be evaluated as error, not as proof about the origin of a cross-modality signal.
And if TransferGate v1 admits ATAC, does that certify the coupling as biological?

Not automatically. Admission reflects whatever conditions the implemented checks and bounds justify. The strongest defensible interpretation depends on whether the applicable donor–batch and perturbation–batch comparisons, controls, and batch-effect assumptions actually exclude the relevant batch-only explanations. A gate decision alone need not establish a unique biological mechanism.
What exactly should the RMSE benchmark compare?

Compare perturbation-response RMSE from the gated RNA–ATAC approach with RNA-only models under comparable holdouts where both donor and perturbation are unseen. The stated predictive target is a relative reduction of at least 15%, equivalent to gated RMSE no greater than 0.85 times RNA-only RMSE on the same evaluation condition. This activity states that the benchmark will be run; it does not report an RMSE result.
Why benchmark the gated approach as a whole rather than just predictions where ATAC was admitted?

The approach includes both decisions to use ATAC and decisions to fall back, so its overall joint-holdout RMSE describes the predictions made under that conditional policy. Admitted cases can raise a separate question, but their RMSE alone would not describe the full gated approach. Neither summary, by itself, tells us whether the underlying coupling is identifiable.
Do I need to report the fallback assessment separately from overall RMSE?

Yes, conceptually. Overall RMSE asks how accurate the predictions are; the fallback assessment asks whether designs that cannot support the intended interpretation are handled without an unjustified ATAC contribution. Low aggregate error could conceal an inappropriate gate decision in an ambiguous design, and a well-justified fallback does not guarantee the required predictive improvement.
What if a design has enough donor overlap but the interaction check raises a concern?

That combination should not be collapsed into a simple claim that overlap resolved batch confounding. Donor crossing supplies contrasts, while donor-by-batch interactions test whether the assumptions used to interpret those contrasts remain adequate. The activity does not specify the exact gate action for every such combination; the benchmark and fallback assessment are intended to keep both interpretive and predictive consequences in view.
What if the controls appear suitable but the perturbation is batch-exclusive?

Then the control diagnostic and the perturbation-incidence result should remain distinct. Suitable controls may constrain a batch-driven accessibility explanation, while a batch-exclusive perturbation still lacks a same-perturbation contrast across batches. TransferGate v1’s stated checks make it possible to describe both facts; this activity does not establish a universal decision or an identifiability conclusion from them alone.
Can a nonidentifiable-design fallback be considered a failed prediction?

No. It is a decision about which information the predictor may rely on, not an error value. Whether its prediction is accurate is measured on the relevant holdout. Calling it a fallback acknowledges a limit on the ATAC-based interpretation; it does not say the response cannot be predicted.
How can the activity address the biological-versus-batch question without overstating what the checks prove?

Describe each check in terms of the ambiguity it probes, and distinguish a diagnostic result from a proof that all alternatives are excluded. Rank and incidence address available contrasts; controls challenge batch-based explanations; interaction checks challenge assumptions about batch effects; transport eligibility concerns use in new prediction settings. When the available information leaves biological and batch-only explanations compatible, the appropriate outcome is a qualified interpretation or fallback, not a claim of uniquely identified coupling.
Is this an evaluation of a global alignment between every RNA and ATAC measurement?

Not as stated. TransferGate v1 is an implementation for conditional RNA–ATAC use in perturbation-response prediction, with checks on when that use is supportable. Its benchmark concerns joint-holdout RMSE, and its fallback assessment concerns nonidentifiable designs. Those aims do not require claiming a uniquely identified correspondence for every unpaired RNA and ATAC observation.
What should I avoid saying before the benchmark is run?

Avoid stating that TransferGate v1 has met the 15% RMSE target, that every allowed ATAC contribution is biologically identifiable, or that its fallbacks have already behaved correctly in all nonidentifiable designs. Implementation and benchmarking are the stated activity; performance and fallback behavior remain outcomes to assess.
Can you give me a compact description of the activity with both evaluation aims intact?

“Implement TransferGate v1 with rank and donor-overlap, control-independence, perturbation-bridging, transport-eligibility, and donor-by-batch interaction checks. Benchmark gated RNA–ATAC against RNA-only for perturbation-response RMSE on joint unseen-donor and unseen-perturbation holdouts, and separately assess whether nonidentifiable designs receive appropriate fallbacks.”
TransferGate v1 packages eligibility checks, RNA-only fallbacks, coupling-bound diagnostics, and joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE reports. How should I describe the artifact as a whole?

Describe TransferGate v1 as a package for conditionally using RNA–ATAC information in perturbation-response prediction and documenting that use. Its eligibility checks address whether ATAC may contribute; its RNA-only fallbacks provide a prediction path when it may not; its coupling-bound diagnostics help assess the basis for interpreting an ATAC contribution; and its joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE reports address predictive error when both donor and perturbation are unseen. The contents alone do not establish that the checks always make the right decision or that a particular RMSE target is met.
Why separate eligibility checks from coupling-bound diagnostics?

An eligibility check concerns a decision: whether a condition permits ATAC to contribute. A coupling-bound diagnostic concerns the evidence and assumptions relevant to that decision, such as whether the bound is informative and trustworthy for the coupling quantity at issue. Packaging both lets a reader distinguish an action taken by the gate from the justification for that action. It does not mean every eligibility decision has been independently validated.
Does the artifact description specify which checks a case must pass?

Not in full. It says TransferGate v1 packages eligibility checks, but does not give their complete decision logic, thresholds, or ordering. You can identify the checks as a component without claiming a particular case passed them or that one check can substitute for another.
What should I say an RNA-only fallback does?

It allows a prediction to rely on RNA alone when the gated approach does not use ATAC. That can preserve a prediction path without treating an uncertain RNA–ATAC relationship as identified. The artifact description does not specify the exact conditions that trigger each fallback or the accuracy of predictions made through it.
Is a fallback the same thing as saying ATAC has no biological information?

No. A fallback is a decision not to use ATAC for the prediction under the applicable eligibility conditions. Biological information might still be present but not sufficiently distinguished from batch-associated alternatives for the intended use. The fallback does not establish that ATAC is biologically empty.
Should a reader infer that all nonidentifiable designs trigger a fallback?

Not solely from the list of packaged components. It tells a reader that RNA-only fallbacks are available, not how every possible design is classified or whether the fallback behavior has been verified in all ambiguous cases. A statement about a specific design would require its eligibility decision and the identifiability assumptions to be made explicit.
What is the role of the coupling-bound diagnostics if the artifact already reports holdout RMSE?

They address a different question. RMSE shows how closely the resulting predictions match held-out perturbation responses. Coupling-bound diagnostics concern what the bounds support about the relationship used to justify ATAC and, in particular, the limits of interpreting that relationship rather than merely using it predictively. Low RMSE cannot demonstrate that a bound covers its intended quantity or excludes the relevant batch-only explanations.
Does the phrase “coupling-bound diagnostics” guarantee a coverage statistic?

No. It names a diagnostic component but does not list the specific statistics it reports. Coverage is one possible concern when assessing bounds, but this artifact description does not give a coverage value, a coverage threshold, or the precise diagnostic fields. It is safest to describe the component without inventing its measurements.
If a bound excludes zero, can the diagnostics label biological coupling as proven?

Not from zero exclusion alone. The interpretation depends on what the coupling quantity represents, whether the bound is valid under the allowed batch effects, and whether zero exclusion actually rules out the relevant batch-only accounts. A diagnostic can help make those conditions visible; it cannot turn an assumption-dependent bound into unconditional proof of biological coupling.
What exactly is joint about the RMSE reports?

They concern donor–perturbation holdouts, meaning the evaluated prediction is for an unseen donor and an unseen perturbation together. That differs from evaluating only an unseen donor or only an unseen perturbation. The reports are therefore relevant to transfer in the combined condition, although the artifact description does not provide numerical RMSE values.
Does the artifact say that RNA-only RMSE is included as a comparison in each report?

It says TransferGate v1 packages joint donor–perturbation holdout RMSE reports, but it does not explicitly describe every column or comparison in those reports. The broader performance requirement is a 15% reduction in perturbation-response RMSE versus RNA-only models on unseen donors and perturbations. To establish that reduction, the gated and RNA-only RMSE values would have to be comparable on the same joint holdout; the artifact description alone does not establish that they are reported for every condition.
So a joint-holdout RMSE report is not automatically a statement that the 15% requirement was achieved?

Correct. The presence of an RMSE report says that predictive error is documented; it does not state its value. A relative reduction of at least 15% would require the gated RMSE to be no more than 0.85 times the corresponding RNA-only RMSE on the same joint holdout. Nothing about packaging the report supplies that comparison or its result.
Could the artifact report a favorable RMSE even if its coupling bounds remain ambiguous?

Conceptually, yes. Predictive accuracy and identification of biological coupling are separate. TransferGate v1 packages both holdout RMSE reports and coupling-bound diagnostics so those questions can be considered separately. A favorable prediction result would not, by itself, eliminate a batch-only explanation that remains compatible with the bound.
Could the reverse happen: informative bounds but no useful predictive gain?

Yes. A bound could help distinguish a coupling quantity under stated assumptions without ensuring that adding ATAC reduces joint-holdout prediction error enough to be useful. The artifact description reports no particular pairing of diagnostic and RMSE outcomes, so neither direction should be assumed.
Would it be accurate to describe the package as automatically resolving donor–batch confounding?

No. Eligibility checks and coupling-bound diagnostics can help make the donor–batch assumptions and their limits explicit. They do not manufacture missing donor–batch comparisons or guarantee that biological coupling can be separated from batch effects in every design. RNA-only fallbacks are consistent with leaving ATAC unused when the basis for using it is inadequate.
What about a case in which donor and batch cannot be distinguished from the available observations?

The cautious interpretation is that an apparent cross-modality relationship should not be presented as uniquely biological on that basis. TransferGate v1’s fallbacks offer a way to make predictions without requiring an ATAC-based coupling claim in such a case. The artifact description does not, however, document a particular case or prove that every ambiguous design has been recognized correctly.
Does packaging a fallback mean the joint-holdout RMSE report is only for cases that used ATAC?

No. The description does not specify whether a report separates ATAC-admitted cases from fallback cases or gives an overall RMSE for the gated approach. It is important not to infer case-by-case ATAC usage or a reporting format merely from the presence of both fallbacks and RMSE reports.
If the reported RMSE were low, could I tell from that number how often the gate used ATAC?

No. An aggregate RMSE is a measure of prediction error, not an admission count. Without separately reported gate decisions, it would not say which predictions used ATAC and which took the RNA-only fallback. Likewise, a low error would not establish that each admission was justified by the bounds.
Should I present TransferGate v1 as a global RNA–ATAC alignment?

The stated artifact is a package of eligibility checks, fallbacks, coupling-bound diagnostics, and holdout RMSE reports. It does not claim a unique alignment of every unpaired RNA and ATAC measurement. Calling it a conditional prediction and diagnostic package keeps its description closer to what is specified.
What does the version label tell us?
“TransferGate v1” is the artifact’s name. It does not, by itself, say anything about other versions, their contents, or future changes.
